articles.title: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet on reforming the bloc - Euronews.com
articles.summary: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet on reforming the bloc  Euronews.com‘No more Viktor Orbán’: EU plans 15-year probation period for new member states  The GuardianEU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members  DW.comEverything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real  The Kyiv IndependentPreparing for a wider European Union  European Commission
articles.full_text:
The European Commission is proposing fewer commissioners and less unanimity to prepare the EU for 30 or more members. However, EU diplomats say capitals are unlikely to agree.
The European Commission has put forward far-reaching proposals, including cutting the number of commissioners and moving away from unanimity, testing member states' appetite for internal reforms that stop short of treaty change.
The proposals are part of a broader package to make the EU's structures and decision-making fit for a membership of 30 or more countries. They are bound to be controversial among European capitals.
"The main question has been: is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible. Our assessment shows that in most policy areas, the EU is already fit for enlargement," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters.
Unanimity
The Commission proposes identifying areas where so-called passerelle clauses could be activated, allowing the Council to move from unanimity to qualified majority. Activating those clauses, however, itself requires unanimity.
The idea of extending qualified majority voting is not new, particularly in foreign and security policy, where a veto can undermine the EU's ability to project geopolitical weight abroad.
Last month, 11 countries including France and Germany circulated a joint letter calling for the bloc to explore curbing obstructive foreign policy vetoes on the basis of sincere cooperation, notably through greater use of constructive abstention.
Asked whether member states back the move, Kos acknowledged that positions differ widely among EU countries. "It will not be easy, but it is worth trying," she said. A specific area she identified where less unanimity could be used is precisely during accession processes.
"Our proposal is to make our decision-making process more effective. We suggest using more QMV [qualified majority voting], which is nothing new. What is new is that we are suggesting that we will reduce the number of unanimity decisions in the accession process," Kos said.
Unanimity is required to grant a country candidate status and to close negotiations. In between, however, the current methodology gives any member state a veto over 150 steps.
The Commission also wants to make more use of enhanced cooperation, which lets at least nine member states pursue deeper integration on matters of crucial or strategic interest where blockages persist.
The most recent examples are the Ukraine Support Loan, from which Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out, and the European Public Prosecutor's Office.
Here too, Brussels may meet resistance from some capitals, notably the so-called "Friends of the Western Balkans", a group that includes Italy and Austria. They have pushed back against differentiated membership and regulatory asymmetry.
Institutional changes
The Commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which could prove problematic in a Union of 30 or more members.
Under the Lisbon Treaty, the Commission should have a number of members equal to two-thirds of the member states, chosen by "strictly equal rotation" that reflects the demographic and geographical range of all EU countries.
The system never took effect. In 2013, the European Council unanimously decided to keep one commissioner per member state, a concession to Ireland to secure a yes vote in its second referendum on the Lisbon Treaty.
Ireland was merely the most vocal opponent of losing a permanent presence in the Commission. Small member states widely fear their voice would be harder to hear in Brussels.
Rotation could also be hard to swallow for large countries such as France and Germany, which might find themselves left out of the College of Commissioners while the likes of Malta or Luxembourg are included.
"There are some candidates who say, no worries, this country can represent us. Other countries who say, yes, but not at the beginning. We would like to see how it [the Commission] works," Kos added.
The proposal for a leaner EU executive is well timed. The Commission is undergoing a so-called "large-scale review", and capitals are in intense talks on the bloc's next long-term budget, in which the EU administration is likely to face deep cuts.
Sceptical reception
Proposals that mainly affect candidate countries, such as safeguards against democratic backsliding and gradual integration, are likely to meet less resistance.
However, supporters of the reforms point out that, as candidates edge closer to joining the bloc, the question of how to keep an enlarged Union effective will be harder to dismiss.
Still, the suggestion is sure to raise eyebrows among European governments. Four EU diplomats who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity said these internal reforms are unlikely to fly.
The first test will come next week, when the enlargement reforms will land on the table of the EU leaders gathered for the European Council on 15-16 October.
"Some things are drafted to be killed," an EU diplomat said.

articles.title: Eurozone inflation just hit 3.8%, its highest in three years. This chart shows why the ECB can’t simply hike its way out - FXStreet
articles.summary: Eurozone inflation just hit 3.8%, its highest in three years. This chart shows why the ECB can’t simply hike its way out  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) would normally have a relatively straightforward answer to inflation running almost twice its target: raise interest rates. But these are not normal circumstances. This time, the bond market is already doing part of the tightening for it, leaving the ECB facing an increasingly difficult dilemma.
Eurozone Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) inflation accelerated to 3.8% YoY in September from 3.2% in August, beating expectations of 3.6% and reaching its highest level in three years. Core inflation also edged higher to 2.5% from 2.4%.
The numbers strengthen the argument that the ECB's inflation fight is not over. Yet, at almost exactly the same time, another form of monetary tightening is taking place without the central bank having to do anything. Government bond yields are soaring.
Germany's 10-year borrowing costs recently reached their highest level in 17 years, while France's 10-year yield approached 5%, its highest since 2002. The spread between French and German government bonds has meanwhile widened sharply amid concerns over France's fiscal outlook, with similar widening also observed in Italian and Spanish sovereign spreads.
Higher market rates feed through into borrowing costs for governments, companies and households, potentially slowing investment and economic activity. The ECB therefore faces an unusual question: if bond markets are already tightening financial conditions, how much further does the central bank itself need to go?
The bond market may be doing part of the ECB's job
The answer matters because the ECB has already raised interest rates twice this year, bringing the Deposit Facility rate to 2.50%. BBH argues that above-target inflation and firmer growth still give the ECB room to tighten further. The swaps curve, according to the bank, implies almost 75 basis points of additional tightening over the coming twelve months. TD Securities also expects another 25-basis-point increase in December, which would take the deposit rate to 2.75%.
But the rapid increase in long-term borrowing costs is beginning to challenge that straightforward hawkish narrative.
Deutsche Bank analysts argue that tighter financial conditions are creating “growing doubt whether central banks like the ECB could hike rates as aggressively as thought.” Standard Chartered reaches a similar conclusion. The bank notes that core inflation has only risen modestly since the beginning of the year and argues that higher yields create downside risks for both economic growth and inflation. As a result, the bank sees limited odds of an October rate increase and expects policymakers to prefer waiting for fresh macroeconomic projections in December.
The mechanism is relatively simple. Central banks raise policy rates partly to make credit more expensive, weaken demand and eventually reduce inflation. But when longer-term bond yields rise sharply on their own, mortgages, corporate financing and government borrowing can become more expensive even without another ECB rate increase. Aviva Investors Senior Portfolio Manager Steve Ryder described the bond sell-off as a potential “circuit breaker for rate expectations.”
That is increasingly becoming the central question facing policymakers. Inflation says tighten. Bond markets are already tightening for them.
Higher yields could actually help bring inflation down
Several ECB policymakers are explicitly acknowledging this dynamic. Governor of the Bank of Finland and member of the ECB Governing Council Olli Rehn said higher energy prices are bringing the Eurozone closer to the ECB's adverse inflation scenario. But he also pointed to the opposite force coming from financial markets. “The rise in long-term interest rates will slow growth and reduce the pass-through of the energy shock to other prices and wages,” said Rehn.
ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel has made a similar argument. She said the economy could respond more strongly than expected to the recent surge in global yields, which “would dampen price pressures.”
ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane reinforced this view, arguing that the rise in long-term interest rates will slow economic growth and reduce the pass-through of the energy shock by more than previously projected. Crucially, Lane said that the “demand destruction” caused by higher energy costs could limit the adjustment required from ECB interest rates.
Nordea economists noted that September's acceleration was mainly driven by energy and food, while broader price pressures remained relatively moderate. The bank therefore does not expect an October rate hike, although it retains forecasts for increases in December and March.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has also emphasized the absence, so far, of clear evidence that the latest inflation shock is becoming embedded. “We see higher inflation ahead but no signs yet that it is becoming embedded,” the ECB President said, arguing that a “measured response” remains appropriate. Phillip Lane, nevertheless, warned that the “second wave” of the energy supply shock creates direct upside risks to inflation while simultaneously posing downside risks to economic growth.
This leaves policymakers waiting for one crucial development: whether the energy shock remains concentrated in headline inflation or begins feeding more aggressively into wages, services and other prices. If second-round effects appear, the argument for higher rates becomes considerably stronger. If they do not, surging bond yields could increasingly substitute for additional ECB tightening.
France makes the ECB's dilemma much more complicated
The problem is that not all European yields are rising for the same reason. Part of the bond sell-off is global. US, UK, German and Japanese borrowing costs have all risen sharply amid concerns about inflation, energy prices, fiscal deficits and the outlook for central-bank policy.
France adds another layer. French 10-year government bond yields recently approached 5%, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt rather than German Bunds has surged to levels not seen since the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis.
That spread matters for the ECB because monetary policy is supposed to transmit throughout the currency union. If borrowing costs rise broadly across the Eurozone because markets expect higher ECB rates, monetary tightening is functioning largely as intended. If borrowing costs in one group of countries begin rising much faster because investors question their fiscal position, the ECB starts facing fragmentation. And tighter policy could make that divergence worse.
MUFG argues that the widening in Eurozone spreads has already begun changing the monetary-policy debate. The bank notes that market pricing for ECB rate increases through mid-2027 has fallen by around 30 basis points from its recent peak as the bond sell-off intensified. ING Global Head of Markets Chris Turner argues that the French debt sell-off has “broken the narrative of ever-higher short-term market interest rates.” According to Turner, the move raises the question of whether central banks risk entering policy-error territory by continuing to tighten while financial conditions are already deteriorating.
That creates a difficult feedback loop. Higher inflation pushes the ECB toward higher rates. Expectations for higher rates contribute to higher bond yields. Higher yields tighten financial conditions and increase pressure on indebted sovereigns. That pressure then reduces the ECB's room to raise rates.
The ECB could eventually face an even bigger contradiction
If sovereign stress continues to increase, the debate could move beyond whether the ECB should raise rates. It could turn toward whether the ECB needs to support the bond market. The central bank created the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) in 2022 to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the Eurozone. The instrument potentially allows the ECB to purchase sovereign bonds from countries facing unjustified market pressure.
But deploying it today would create an obvious communication challenge. The ECB is raising interest rates because inflation is too high. Purchasing government bonds to suppress borrowing costs would simultaneously ease financial conditions in parts of the economy.
Bloomberg describes this possibility as a potential “nightmare scenario” for the central bank. The issue is particularly sensitive in France because the rise in the country's risk premium is at least partly linked to its fiscal position.
“The spread widening is warranted given the fiscal stance and political uncertainty,” says Danske Bank Chief Strategist Piet Christiansen. Adding: “That's also what complicates the market view on the ECB. If it hampers monetary-policy transmission, it's a job for the ECB. If not, let's let the market price the drivers without intervening.”
That distinction could determine whether the TPI can realistically be deployed. The ECB designed the instrument to address unjustified fragmentation, not to shield governments from higher borrowing costs caused by their own fiscal fundamentals.
Bundesbank President and ECB Governing Council member Joachim Nagel has pushed back against expectations that specific spread levels could automatically trigger intervention. “My job in the Governing Council is to fulfill my mandate. It has nothing to do with maybe certain spread levels or things like that. It's price stability,” noted Nagel.
Three imperfect choices for the ECB
The ECB therefore appears to be moving toward a situation in which every available option carries a cost. It can continue raising rates aggressively to prevent the energy shock from spreading into underlying inflation. That could protect its inflation-fighting credibility, but also push borrowing costs higher, weaken growth and potentially amplify fragmentation across sovereign bond markets.

articles.full_text:
China will monitor the United Kingdom’s moves on tariffs targeting Chinese electric vehicles and respond accordingly, as London considers whether to introduce new trade measures against Chinese-made EVs. The issue has emerged amid growing concerns in Britain and other major economies over Chinese industrial capacity, government support and the competitive pressure facing domestic automakers.
Beijing’s position comes as the UK weighs possible tariffs on Chinese electric cars. British officials have been consulting industry representatives over potential measures, but the UK has not yet formally imposed a new China-specific tariff on electric vehicles. Any decision would therefore represent a shift in Britain’s current trade approach toward Chinese EV imports.
China has increasingly objected to what it regards as protectionist restrictions on its electric-vehicle exports. Its Commerce Ministry has previously said measures restricting Chinese EVs should comply with World Trade Organization rules and has opposed what it considers discriminatory trade barriers.
In January, China’s Commerce Ministry said Beijing and the European Union had made progress in consultations over the EU’s anti-subsidy case concerning Chinese battery-electric vehicles. The ministry said both sides had agreed that Chinese exporters could pursue price commitments as a way of addressing European concerns within the WTO framework.
China has also taken steps to regulate its own electric-vehicle exports. Since January 1, 2026, China has required export licences for pure-electric passenger vehicles, under rules introduced by the Commerce Ministry, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, General Administration of Customs and State Administration for Market Regulation. Beijing said the system was intended to promote the healthy development of new-energy vehicle trade and regulate export activity.
The UK’s position is complicated by its broader industrial policy. London has been reviewing its zero-emission vehicle strategy while seeking to support domestic manufacturing and investment. The government said in August that more than one in four new cars sold in Britain were electric and that EV sales had risen 45% year-on-year in July. It also launched a review of the pathway toward its target for all new cars and vans to be zero-emission by 2035.
The potential tariff debate reflects a wider global argument over the competitivenes

articles.title: UK weighs EV tariffs on China as Beijing signals a response could follow - Business Upturn
articles.summary: UK weighs EV tariffs on China as Beijing signals a response could follow  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
The UK is taking a fresh look at tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The move could open another trade battle between Britain and China. Beijing is already watching closely.
According to a report from First Squawk, China will monitor the UK's move on electric vehicle tariffs and respond accordingly. The warning comes at a sensitive time for the British car industry. Chinese EV brands have been growing quickly in the UK market.
The UK currently charges a 10% import duty on Chinese electric vehicles. That is much lower than the additional duties imposed by the European Union on Chinese EVs. The possibility of higher UK tariffs could therefore change the way Chinese carmakers approach the British market.
UK EV tariffs on Chinese cars
The British government has not officially announced a new tariff on Chinese electric vehicles yet. Instead, officials are considering their options.
The issue has become more important because Chinese carmakers have gained a much bigger presence in the UK. Brands such as BYD, Chery, Omoda and Jaecoo have been expanding their sales. Chinese brands accounted for more than 20% of new EV sales in the UK in September, according to recent reporting.
Britain is also facing pressure from Europe. The European Union already applies additional anti subsidy duties to Chinese electric vehicles. These duties vary depending on the manufacturer and are added to the normal import duty.
This puts the UK in a difficult position.
If Britain keeps its lower tariff, Chinese EV makers could find the UK more attractive than other European markets. That could bring cheaper electric cars to British consumers. It could also put more pressure on local manufacturers.
At the same time, higher tariffs could make Chinese electric vehicles more expensive. That could reduce competition and make it harder for consumers to find lower priced EVs.
The British government has already said it is concerned about overcapacity and market distorting practices. In July, officials said they were assessing possible measures, including tariffs, but stressed that any action would need to serve UK industry. At that point, the Trade Remedies Authority had not started an investigation into Chinese EVs.
China could respond to UK EV tariffs
China's latest warning adds another layer to the issue.
If the UK introduces higher tariffs on Chinese EVs, Beijing could consider measures of its own. The exact response is not known. It could depend on how large the British tariff is and which Chinese products or companies are affected.
That possibility is important for Britain because its relationship with China goes beyond electric cars.
British companies sell a wide range of goods and services into international markets. The automotive sector also depends on complicated global supply chains. Any major trade dispute could therefore create problems beyond the showroom.
Jaguar Land Rover is one company being watched closely. The British carmaker has significant exposure to international markets, including China. UK officials have reportedly been concerned that retaliation from Beijing could hurt British exporters.
There is another complication.
Some Chinese carmakers are not simply looking to export vehicles into Britain. They are also considering investment and local production. That means tariffs could affect future factory plans as well as current vehicle prices.
The British government therefore has to balance several interests at once. It wants to protect local manufacturers. It also wants to attract investment. At the same time, it does not want to make electric vehicles unnecessarily expensive for British buyers.
China UK trade tensions could grow
The latest development also shows how complicated the global EV market has become.
China has become a major force in electric vehicles. Its manufacturers have built strong positions in batteries, technology and vehicle production. European countries and the United States have responded with trade measures designed to protect their own industries.
Britain now has to decide how closely it wants to follow that approach.
The decision could also affect the UK's relationship with the European Union. European officials have been pushing Britain to take tougher action against Chinese EV imports. There are concerns that the UK could otherwise become a route for Chinese vehicles into the wider European market.
For British consumers, the outcome could eventually be felt in car prices. Higher tariffs generally raise the cost of imported products. But stronger competition can also pressure manufacturers to keep prices down.
That creates a difficult choice for policymakers.
For China, the issue is equally important. Chinese automakers have been expanding overseas at a rapid pace. Losing easier access to another major market could affect that expansion. Beijing's response will therefore be closely watched if London moves ahead with new tariffs.
For now, the key point is that the UK has not yet imposed the new tariffs. The government is still weighing its options. China, however, has already made clear that it will be watching what Britain does next.
The next move from London could decide whether this remains a policy debate or turns into another major trade dispute. If the UK raises tariffs, the biggest question will not only be how Chinese EV makers react, but whether Beijing chooses to target British exports in return. That could turn Britain's EV tariff decision into a much wider test of its trade relationship with China.

articles.title: Expert fears UK and Europe ‘will wake up only after capitals are hit’ then ‘it’s too late’ - London Business News
articles.summary: Expert fears UK and Europe ‘will wake up only after capitals are hit’ then ‘it’s too late’  London Business News
articles.full_text:
Russia is testing how far it can pressure Europe without triggering a direct military confrontation, as drone incursions, sabotage and cyber operations increasingly blur the boundary between peace and war.
The pattern of incidents has prompted European officials and security experts to reassess whether Moscow’s activities should be viewed as isolated acts of hybrid warfare or as part of a sustained campaign designed to probe the limits of Europe’s response.
Recent allegations have included Russian-linked sabotage, cyberattacks and violations of European airspace. Germany has warned of an intensifying Russian “shadow war”, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has accused Moscow of putting lives at risk through hybrid operations across Europe. Russia has denied such allegations.
The concern is not necessarily that Moscow is preparing an immediate conventional assault on NATO. Rather, European officials increasingly fear that Russia can exert pressure through actions that fall below the threshold at which governments would consider a military response.
Read more related news:
Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert, describes the pattern as a “sub-threshold war” against Europe.
The distinction matters because traditional deterrence is easier to apply when an attack is unambiguous. A missile strike against a NATO country would create a clear basis for collective defence. A cyberattack, suspected act of sabotage or drone incursion presents governments with a more difficult calculation over attribution, proportionality and escalation.
Leopold Schmertzing, a strategic foresight and security and defence policy expert, argues that Moscow’s campaign aims to weaken the European political model as well as its physical infrastructure.
“Russia is waging a war against the European model of freedom, equality, and solidarity, and against the institutions that sustain it, especially the EU. This is a war fought in small steps,” he said.
“I struggle to see it ending without a fundamental change in either the current Russian model or the European one.”
European governments have nevertheless strengthened their defences substantially since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The EU has identified air and missile defence, drones and counter-drone systems, cyber capabilities, communications, intelligence and command structures among its key capability gaps.
Air defence has become particularly important as European countries confront the proliferation of relatively inexpensive unmanned systems. Recent Russian drone activity has prompted NATO countries to scramble aircraft and accelerate investment in cheaper counter-drone technologies.
Ukraine’s battlefield experience has provided an unusually direct demonstration of the changing economics of warfare. Drones can conduct reconnaissance, identify targets and attack military infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of many traditional weapons systems.
Kateryna Mykhalko, managing director of the German-Ukrainian defence industry consortium New Age Defence, argues that European spending has yet to fully reflect that transformation.
“That is how the modern war looks like,” she said. “At the same time, the technology delivering 80% of battlefield results receives only roughly 2% of European defence budgets.”
Europe is attempting to close part of that gap through industrial co-operation with Ukraine. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance, formally launched in July, brings European and Ukrainian companies together to develop drones and counter-drone systems, with the stated aim of combining Ukrainian battlefield experience with European industrial capacity.
The challenge extends beyond hardware. Europe must also improve the communications, intelligence, surveillance and command systems required to operate military capabilities collectively. EU assessments have identified persistent shortfalls in strategic collective capabilities and command-and-control structures, potentially limiting the ability of European states to sustain a prolonged military response.
For Schmertzing, the central danger is that Europe could underestimate the cumulative effect of incidents that individually fall short of conventional warfare.
“My fear is that we will only fully wake up when our own capitals are attacked and our citizens are killed. By then, it will be too late to prepare,” he said.
That creates a difficult strategic problem. Europe must strengthen deterrence without turning every act of sabotage or airspace violation into a trigger for uncontrolled escalation.
The result is an increasingly contested space between war and peace, in which Moscow can test European resilience while European governments attempt to demonstrate that the threshold for coercion is not infinitely low.
The question for Europe is therefore not simply whether Russia will launch a conventional attack. It is whether the continent can close the vulnerabilities exposed by the conflict in Ukraine quickly enough to make the incremental pressure of a shadow war less effective.
As Schmertzing puts it: “Russia is a hard nut to crack because it is deeply vulnerable in some respects and remarkably insulated in others.”
“We have a great deal to learn from Ukraine about where pressure works and where it doesn’t.”
Last month NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte said he will not publicly disclose the precise circumstances that could trigger its collective-defence commitment, he warned, saying revealing the alliance’s threshold would allow adversaries to calculate how far they could escalate without provoking a response.
“Article 5 is deliberately ambiguous, so we will never exactly tell anyone when Article 5 is exactly triggered or not,” Rutte said during a discussion on the future of NATO and the alliance’s importance to US security.
The comments come as NATO faces growing concern over Russia’s use of cyberattacks, sabotage, disinformation, drone incursions and other forms of hybrid activity aimed at testing the alliance without crossing an obvious conventional military threshold.
Rutte said NATO had “all the response options we need” to deal with hybrid threats, but stressed that some measures could remain secret.
As Russia continues to probe the boundaries between peace and conflict, the alliance is deliberately keeping its most important red line unwritten.

articles.title: Euro plummets to a 17-month low against US dollar: Has the next financial crisis begun? - DW.com
articles.summary: Euro plummets to a 17-month low against US dollar: Has the next financial crisis begun?  DW.com
articles.full_text:
The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns about eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices.
The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down about 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 (€0.99) on Monday, the lowest level since early 2025.
Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist at Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields.
However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk."
The France problem
The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly.
France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion).
France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office.
For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt.
The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely watched measure of EU financial stability.
What can the ECB do?
The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic.
Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand.
"The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said.
Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added.
He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now.
What is at stake?
Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability.
Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the leading candidate.
Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy.
Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament.
Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation.
"Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said.
A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods, particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports.
The next financial crisis?
With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone.
Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believe such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.
However, Amaro says the fact that further interest rate hikes are expected from the ECB this year, combined with the worsening inflation outlook, makes this a situation which needs to be managed and monitored very carefully.
"Euro weakness shouldn't be interpreted as an isolated development," he says. "If triggered by growing concerns about France's fiscal outlook, then the ECB would certainly want to thread that carefully given risks for the eurozone."
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title: ‘All-in' Russia invasion warning as NATO's two major weaknesses exposed - AOL.com
articles.summary: ‘All-in' Russia invasion warning as NATO's two major weaknesses exposed  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
Russia would have to go "all-in" if it were to launch an incursion into Estonia, an expert has said. There has been speculation over recent days at to whether the Kremlin could orchestrate a takeover of part of the Baltic country. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggested that Russian agents would take over major buildings in Narva. Experts also pointed out that long-range drones could be launched from Russia.
Merili Arjakas, a research fellow at The International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) - a think tank in Estonia specialising in security, defence and foreign policy issues - and the editor-in-chief of foreign policy magazine Diplomaatia, told The Express: "Russia cannot expect that any such attack against Estonia or the Baltic states will remain limited, as if the European states had not learned anything from the annexation in Crimea and the war in Donbas, which led to the full-scale invasion eight years later.
"That is not to say that Russia is not an aggressive power or that Putin does not dream of the collapse of NATO. Rather, any incursion will face a strong and immediate response from us and our partners."
A small-scale operation would not be sufficient, Ms Arjakas suggested.
She said: "Therefore, if I were Russia and I wanted to attack Estonia or the Baltics, I would go all-in, not think that any limited incursion to Narva or to other places would be enough.
"Fortunately for us, Russia has so far been careful to not create conditions for a large-scale confrontation with NATO. Its tolerance of such risk has certainly increased as they carry out more attacks that fall below the threshold for triggering Article 5.
"However, such asymmetric escalation is also characteristic of a weaker party, one that still deems it too risky to use conventional means."
Estonia is "taking the threat seriously", the specialist added, while also pointing major NATO weaknesses.
"Our defence budget for 2026 is 5.4% of GDP (€2.4billion), with major spending on ammunition, medium-range air defence, HIMARS, UAVs, anti-tank systems and territorial defence," Ms Arjakas said.
"Similar investments have been done by Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, while Finland has long been a shining example of a country armed to the teeth and prepared to fight.
"There are vulnerabilities - particularly in defence against missiles and drones, as well as in terms of reinforcement and logistics in the event of a full-scale invasion. But these are not vulnerabilities unique to Estonia or the eastern flank; rather, they are shared by all NATO countries except the US.
"Our best way of avoiding a NATO-Russia war, whether it erupts here or elsewhere, is still to support Ukraine so the aggressor does not prevail there. Ukraine keeps Russian forces and resources tied down and degrades Russian military capacity, thereby not only fighting for its own survival and sovereignty but also acting as a shield for Europe."

articles.title: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to align with EU industrial policy - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: UK weighs tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to align with EU industrial policy  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom government is actively evaluating the imposition of import tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, marking a significant potential shift in post-Brexit trade strategy. The move is reportedly being considered to align British policy with the European Union, thereby strengthening the UK’s case for inclusion in the bloc’s forthcoming industrial protection legislation designed to shield domestic manufacturing from subsidized foreign competition.
According to industry reports and diplomatic sources, the EU has directly raised the question of tariff alignment with UK officials during ongoing negotiations surrounding the "Made in Europe" framework, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA represents a cornerstone of the European Commission’s strategy to revitalize the continent's industrial base, requiring manufacturers to procure components locally and imposing strict conditions on third countries seeking access to its protected supply chains. Brussels maintains that for the UK to qualify for inclusion in this scheme and benefit from a level playing field, it must mirror the punitive tariffs of up to 45 percent that the EU levied on Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles in October 2024.
Currently, the UK stands as a notable outlier among major Western economies in its refusal to enact blanket import taxes on Chinese automotive products. While the United States has effectively shut out Chinese EVs through aggressive trade barriers, and the EU has implemented targeted anti-subsidy duties following a lengthy investigation, the previous UK administration maintained a more open market approach. The prevailing argument in Westminster has historically been that Britain does not require the same protective trade barriers as the EU, largely because the UK does not suffer from the same massive trade deficit in goods that Brussels is struggling to contain.
However, the risk assessment within Whitehall has reportedly evolved. Senior government sources indicate that the impending implementation of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act poses a direct threat to the British automotive sector. The UK car industry remains deeply integrated with European supply chains, and the EU remains the largest export market for finished British vehicles and components. If the UK is excluded from the "Made in Europe" provisions due to its failure to impose equivalent tariffs on Chinese imports, domestic manufacturers could face severe competitive disadvantages, potentially leading to production shifts and job losses within the UK.
Implementing such tariffs, however, is not a straightforward administrative decision. Any unilateral imposition of import duties would likely trigger a hostile response from Beijing, complicating broader diplomatic and trade relations at a time when the UK is seeking to stabilize its post-Brexit international partnerships. Furthermore, establishing legally defensible tariffs requires a rigorous process through the World Trade Organization (WTO). The EU’s own investigation into state subsidies within the Chinese EV supply chain took 13 months to conclude before duties could be lawfully applied. The UK would need to conduct its own trade remedy investigation, gathering evidence of market distortion and economic injury to domestic producers, a process that could delay the implementation of any new duties well into the future.
The political dynamics surrounding this decision are equally complex. The current government has previously positioned itself as pragmatic regarding Chinese investment, viewing it as a potential driver of economic growth rather than solely a systemic risk to British manufacturing. A pivot toward protectionist tariffs would represent a stark departure from that rhetoric, signaling a prioritization of domestic industrial security over consumer access to low-cost green technology. Consumer advocates and environmental groups have previously warned that tariffs on Chinese EVs could artificially inflate vehicle prices, potentially slowing the UK’s transition to zero-emission transport and complicating the achievement of national climate targets.
European industry leaders, particularly within the automotive and chemicals sectors, have lobbied intensely for a unified front against the influx of heavily subsidized Chinese exports. They argue that without coordinated tariffs, European and British manufacturers cannot compete on price, regardless of their technological advancements. The UK’s participation in the IAA’s supply chain requirements would mandate that a significant percentage of vehicle components be sourced from within the UK or the EU, a stipulation designed to rebuild regional industrial capacity and reduce reliance on Asian supply networks.
The Industrial Accelerator Act encompasses strategic industries beyond automotive, including green hydrogen and advanced chemicals. For the UK’s chemical sectors, exclusion from the IAA’s preferential treatment could divert foreign direct investment toward EU member states. Multinational corporations planning new gigafactories may bypass the UK if it cannot offer guaranteed access to the protected European market. Furthermore, imposing anti-subsidy duties under WTO rules requires the UK’s Trade Remedies Authority (TRA) to initiate a formal probe, demonstrating a link between foreign financial contributions and material injury to domestic industry. This evidentiary burden ensures tariffs are grounded in rigorous economic analysis, though the process invites intense scrutiny from both Beijing and Brussels.
The environmental implications present a significant policy paradox. While the UK is committed to phasing out internal combustion engines, the affordability of EVs remains a barrier to mass adoption. Chinese manufacturers leverage state-backed supply chains to produce EVs at a fraction of European costs. Imposing a 45 percent tariff would pass costs onto consumers, potentially stalling the EV market and undermining carbon reduction commitments. Policymakers are exploring alternative mechanisms, such as localized battery manufacturing incentives, to offset the price differential without resorting to blunt import taxes.
As the deadline for the finalization of the Industrial Accelerator Act approaches, the pressure on Whitehall to declare its position is intensifying. The outcome of these deliberations will not only dictate the price of cars on British driveways but will fundamentally reshape the UK’s integration into European industrial policy for decades to come.

articles.title: NATO is preparing a "theory of victory" with drones and AI to repel a Russian attack - Bloomberg - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.summary: NATO is preparing a "theory of victory" with drones and AI to repel a Russian attack - Bloomberg  Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.full_text:
Kyiv • UNN
Hrynkevych will present a strategy for rapidly repelling a Russian attack in Poland. NATO plans to combine traditional forces with drones and AI.
NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy to achieve a swift victory against a Russian attack on the alliance’s eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies, such as drones and artificial intelligence, into traditional defense. Bloomberg reported, UNN writes.
Details
The document, titled "Theory of Victory," which the publication reviewed in an unclassified form, will be presented by NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, in Poland on October 12, amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia.
According to senior officials and diplomats familiar with the matter, it aims to clarify how the alliance would respond to a possible invasion of NATO territory. There have recently been numerous reports that Moscow is considering such actions, the publication writes.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently said there were no signs that Russia was preparing for a conventional attack on the alliance, but Europe must be prepared for sustained hybrid attacks.
Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Colonel Martin O’Donnell, declined to discuss the plan’s details but emphasized that the alliance is "purely defensive."
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s ‘Theory of Victory’ is simple: preserve NATO’s advantage," O’Donnell said. "Given the unstable and complex global security situation, we need to create the conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, prevail in the event of an attack."
Although the general principles of NATO’s approach to warfare are known, open discussion of them is rare, the publication notes. The initiative is intended to reassure the public about NATO’s readiness while also presenting a more concrete picture of what lies behind increased defense spending.
The document also aims to illustrate to allies how NATO will integrate conventional weapons with new capabilities that have emerged since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as call for increased investment in defense and better preparedness, sources said.
The strategy insists on NATO’s defensive nature and avoiding unintended provocations, while clearly mentioning the need for collective action against hybrid threats – aggressive actions below the threshold of conflict – as part of deterrence. By demonstrating readiness, NATO wants the adversary to conclude that it cannot win, the strategy says.
"But if NATO were attacked, it would block the invasion through a combination of ground forces and other resources from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept based on low-cost unmanned vehicles, minimally crewed systems, and artificial-intelligence-based targeting. Once it had freedom of maneuver, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control in order to achieve a rapid and overwhelming defeat of Russian forces," the publication says.
NATO allies, particularly in Europe, have significantly increased defense spending, and tensions have arisen over how to prioritize conventional weapons, such as tanks, versus alternative technologies that have come to the forefront in the war in Ukraine, the publication writes.
This summer, the United States sent NATO allies a questionnaire assessing their defense spending and support for the policies of U.S. President Donald Trump, in order to inform decisions on a planned reduction in U.S. military assets allocated to the defense of Europe.
As part of the questionnaire, the United States asked whether the allies still had forces that could be made available to NATO for Grynkewich’s defense plans, the publication notes.

articles.title: Is France’s Debt Crisis Becoming a Problem for the Euro? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Is France’s Debt Crisis Becoming a Problem for the Euro?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
The euro has come under renewed pressure as concerns over France’s deteriorating public finances and political uncertainty increasingly spill into broader European markets.
The common currency fell to a 17 month low on Monday, declining around 0.7% against the dollar as investors reacted to mounting concerns about France’s high debt levels and political gridlock ahead of next year’s presidential election.
The move came as the US dollar strengthened despite weaker than expected US jobs data, which reduced expectations of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month. Still elevated US Treasury yields continued to support the dollar, widening pressure on the euro.
Why Is France Weighing on the Euro?
France’s fiscal position has become an increasingly important concern for investors. High government debt, persistent budget pressures and political uncertainty have raised questions about Paris’s ability to put public finances on a more sustainable path.
The widening spread between French and German government bond yields has become a key indicator of those concerns. Germany’s bonds are generally treated as a benchmark for the euro zone, meaning a growing gap can signal that investors are demanding a higher premium to hold French debt.
That divergence matters beyond France. If concerns over French borrowing costs intensify, financial markets could begin reassessing risks across the wider euro zone, particularly at a time when European governments are already facing pressure over growth, fiscal policy and geopolitical spending.
What Does This Mean for the European Central Bank?
The weakness of the euro also complicates the policy environment for the European Central Bank.
A weaker currency can make European exports more competitive, but it can also increase the cost of imported goods and energy. For the ECB, the challenge is balancing inflation risks against weak economic growth while financial markets remain sensitive to sovereign debt concerns.
The situation is particularly significant because monetary policy cannot directly resolve the underlying political and fiscal problems facing individual member states. Fiscal credibility remains primarily a responsibility of national governments.
Why Are Investors Watching Japan and the US?
The euro’s decline came against a broader backdrop of shifting expectations about interest rates and government bond markets.
In the United States, investors were pricing in less than a 20% chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase in October, while a December move remained possible. The combination of changing rate expectations and still elevated Treasury yields continued to influence currency markets.
Japan was also in focus after the country’s 30 year government bond yield reached a record high. Investors were awaiting remarks from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi as parliament opened an extraordinary session, with markets watching for signals on the government’s response to economic and financial developments.
What Else Is Moving Markets?
Global equities remained relatively positive, with Asian markets gaining despite thinner trading because of holidays in China, South Korea and Australia’s New South Wales.
Brazil was also in focus after the first round of its presidential election, while investors awaited the runoff later this month between Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
In Sri Lanka, the International Monetary Fund said it had reached a staff level agreement on the seventh review of the country’s Extended Fund Facility, potentially unlocking about $345 million in financing once the review is completed through the required process.
What Should Investors Watch Next?
European markets will be looking closely at September services and composite purchasing managers’ indexes from France and Germany, along with euro zone producer price data for August.
For the euro, however, the bigger question is whether concerns about France remain contained within its sovereign bond market or develop into a broader challenge for confidence in the currency bloc.
The widening gap between French and German borrowing costs will therefore remain an important signal. If that spread continues to increase, investors could face renewed questions about fiscal fragmentation within the euro zone and the ability of European policymakers to contain market pressure.
With information from Reuters.

articles.summary: Donald Trump says he will speak with Vladimir Putin about pneumonic plague  Financial TimesThe plague may have escaped from a lab in Siberia  The EconomistUKHSA says risk of plague 'very low' after Russian laboratory worker 'dies of suspected pneumonic plague'  Sky NewsPlague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says  The Guardian'Black death plague kills second victim' as officials scramble to deny outbreak  Daily Star
articles.full_text:
Your guide to what Trump’s second term means for Washington, business and the world
Donald Trump said he was scheduled to speak with Vladimir Putin about the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia “very soon”, as Washington has urged Moscow to share more about the incident.
The US president on Tuesday said he would speak with his Russian counterpart after US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the White House has received “limited information” on the situation.
Trump on Tuesday declined to provide more information on when the call would take place, but added the US’s intelligence agencies are “in very deep discussions” about the suspected case of the plague. “We’ll be able to report about it probably tomorrow,” he added.
Russia has imposed sweeping quarantine measures in the Siberian region after an employee at Siberia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute was admitted to hospital outside the city a week ago.
Daria Shipilova, 28, died two days later from what public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor described as “pneumonia of unknown” origin. Local media reported pneumonic plague may have been the cause of death.
Rubio earlier on Tuesday called on Moscow for increased transparency.
“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “That’s what they should do, that’s what we hope they will do. And the more we can learn about what happened, the better all of us can be in a position of responding.”
“Maybe there’s nothing there, maybe it’s bigger than we thought, we don’t know,” Rubio added. “Suffice it to say we’re watching it very closely.”
The US secretary of state on Monday said it appeared a worker at the Siberian lab was infected, though he added he did not believe the apparent case was “cause for alarm”.
If confirmed, it would be the first case of plague in a decade in Russia, which has insisted there has been no outbreak.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov urged reporters on Monday “not to listen to rumours about a plague outbreak” and to “rely on Rospotrebnadzor’s statement”.
Trump had said Washington would be willing to help Moscow with the situation.
“We’ll help. Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help,” he said on Monday.

articles.title: MI6 fears German spy chief leaked British secrets - The Telegraph
articles.summary: MI6 fears German spy chief leaked British secrets  The TelegraphFormer German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason  BBCGermany’s beleaguered spies face a fresh scandal  Financial TimesGermany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying  The GuardianFormer German spy chief arrested on espionage allegations  Sky News
articles.full_text:
British intelligence agencies are investigating whether their classified information or spies were compromised in the biggest espionage scandal in modern German history.
August Hanning – the former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service – and a current senior official at the agency, named only as Manfred D, were arrested on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage and treason.
Mr Hanning is accused of illegally collecting classified documents for 16 years through Manfred D and selling some of the secrets to a foreign power.
German security sources said some of the high-level information the pair handled came from partner intelligence agencies abroad, raising the prospect that British and US intelligence had been compromised.
It has also raised fears that US and British human sources, either agents or informants operating in the field, could be identified through information that has been shared.
News of the scandal has shocked the Western intelligence community, with sources describing the alleged breach as a major coup for a foreign power and potentially deeply damaging to the Western intelligence-sharing alliance.
MI6 and GCHQ, as well as several US agencies, are now believed to be undergoing a systematic internal review of all sensitive information shared with European allies during the relevant period.
The Telegraph understands that their primary focus is understood to be safeguarding sources who may have been put at risk by the alleged leak. Similar audits are likely to be undertaken by all Germany’s intelligence-sharing partners and allies.

articles.title: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK  The GuardianWest Midlands hauliers raise prices amid soaring fuel costs  BBCSchool coaches face the axe as diesel prices soar  The TelegraphThe price is…wrong, really wrong  Builders Merchants JournalFishermen 'stuck in port watching' subsidised EU boats as latest fuel surge bites  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
As fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas.
In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise.
While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate.
Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children.
“You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says.
In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay.
“It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says.
About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, most on the largest island, Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders.
“The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says.
Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry.
“You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says.
Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work.
“Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.”
Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back.
“A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says.
Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage. With almost no public transport, he says he needs to drive to work because of how rural it is. The cost of his commute has meant sacrificing some of the things he likes to do with his girlfriend.
“Me and my girlfriend like to go to restaurants that are a bit of a distance away, around half an hour drive. We’ve not done that in a while. I think it’s safe to say that the cost of fuel will be affecting businesses because they’ll be getting fewer customers,” he says.
As fuel costs rise, islanders have started taking jerry cans to the mainland to stock up on cheaper fuel, even to just save a few pennies a litre, Ryan says. Normally, the cans are used in the winter to stock up when high winds and choppy seas disrupt deliveries to the islands and pumps run dry.
“It’s not often that diesel hits the £2 mark, let along £2.17 or whatever it is now. Whenever people say they’re going to the mainland, they say: ‘We’re going to make sure we will take our jerry cans if we are allowed,’” he says. “Even in Skye, the price of petrol and diesel is about 20p cheaper. So, a lot of people actually take the opportunity when they go down to really stock up on fuel whenever they can.”
But even with the cost of living pressures, Ryan is not considering leaving. He says that people are pulling together in the latest surge of inflation.
“People have a romantic view of the islands as being this quiet paradise where you can really get away from it all. But island life is quite hard, especially when costs are rising so significantly,” he says. “But it’s a nice place with a communal feeling. I think that’s what’s getting people through the situation. Everyone is in it together.”

articles.title: 2 Killed in Massive Ukrainian Drone Attack on Moscow - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: 2 Killed in Massive Ukrainian Drone Attack on Moscow  The Moscow TimesMoscow comes under large-scale drone attack – photos, videos  Українська правдаUkrainian drones kill two, hit fuel hub in one of biggest attacks on Moscow region, Russian war bloggers say  ReutersUkraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two  Al JazeeraUkraine preparing for Russian aerial attack, launches nearly 900 drones  Global News
articles.full_text:
A massive Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region overnight killed two people and ignited a fire at a major fuel depot overnight, authorities said, and media reported Tuesday.
A 20-year-old man was killed in the village of Radumlya north of Moscow, while rescuers recovered the body of a 71-year-old man from under the rubble of a destroyed home in Barybino to the south.
Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov confirmed the fatalities and said that nine people were injured in the attack. Forty-seven private homes and four apartment buildings were damaged across seven municipalities, Vorobyov said, ordering local authorities to speed up reconstruction efforts.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “a majority” of the 650 drones launched toward the Russian capital had been intercepted, 105 of them on their immediate approach to Moscow. He reported dozens more interceptions in rapid succession on Tuesday morning.
The exiled outlet Astra reported that video of one of the attacks showed a fire at the Moscow region’s largest fuel storage hub: the Volodarskaya line production and dispatch station. The Moscow Times could not independently verify the report.
The Transneft-owned facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products per year and directly supplies fuel to Moscow’s main airports: Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Vnukovo. According to Astra, the Volodarskaya station has not been a previous target of Ukrainian attacks.
Severe delays and flight cancellations were reported at Sheremetyevo International Airport during the overnight air raid alerts.
The attack follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s weekend pledge to target Russian energy infrastructure in response to Moscow’s intensified air campaign against Ukrainian cities.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 868 Ukrainian drones over dozens of Russian regions overnight.
It said its forces conducted retaliatory strikes against cargo ships and port infrastructure in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports of Chornomorsk and Izmail, as well as digital data centers across several major Ukrainian cities.
On Sunday, the Russian Defense Ministry said it would intensify strikes on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine in response to Zelensky’s pledge.
Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title: Britain is on 'thin ice,' warns ex-Bank of England chief economist — and it must act to 'appease financial markets' - CNBC
articles.summary: Britain is on 'thin ice,' warns ex-Bank of England chief economist — and it must act to 'appease financial markets'  CNBCAndy Burnham must ‘take knife to public spending’ to calm bond markets  The TelegraphUK on ‘thin ice’ over budget tax rises, Andy Burnham warned  The TimesWhy Britain Is Walking A Financial Tightrope Right Now  ИФЗ РАНFormer Bank of England chief economist urges government to cut spending — CNBC  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
The U.K. is "on thin ice" ahead of its critical Autumn Budget, according to a former chief economist of the Bank of England, who warned the government must curb public spending and refrain from painful tax hikes.
Speaking to CNBC's Steve Sedgwick, Andy Haldane — a member of the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee until 2021 — said there were "perils" running into the budget update, currently scheduled for Oct. 28.
"The truth is we are skating on pretty thin ice in fiscal terms, and nothing would be worse both economically and politically than if the ice were to crack beneath our feet," Haldane said on the sidelines of the How Britain Can Win conference, hosted by Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses UK.
Asked if the metaphorical ice is going to crack, he responded that there is "a risk of that" happening. The "single most effective way" to head off such an event, he added, would be for the government to "appease financial markets" by showing it is "able and willing to take the knife to public spending."
"That is the Achilles' heel of this government," Haldane told CNBC. "Unless and until action is taken on that, [Prime Minister Andy Burnham] will remain, alas, in hock to the bond market."
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister over the summer, has previously criticized the U.K.'s fiscal policy as being "in hock" to bond traders.
His emergence as the frontrunner to oust Starmer rattled bond markets earlier this year, with investors perceiving Burnham as much more left-leaning than his predecessor.
With yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, surging amid domestic and global instability in recent years, Britain now has the highest government borrowing costs in the G7.
'History is not on our side'
While Haldane noted that international bond markets had created a "hostile environment for all government borrowers," he said the U.K. was particularly impacted because the country is "a leveraged bet on the world economy."
"Our inflation is higher and stickier. Our growth is lower and stickier. We have yet to balance the books this century — so history is not on our side. The facts are not on our side. That's why the ice is thin."
Haldane said Burnham's push to end the U.K.'s so-called triple lock mechanism — where the state pension rises at the same rate as the highest of inflation, average earnings growth, or 2.5% — was a "good first instalment." But he added that welfare remains a "totemic issue" for the governing Labour party and the bond market.
Gilt markets came under pressure last year when Starmer's finance minister Rachel Reeves watered down her initial plans to cut welfare spending last year, following a revolt from backbench MPs.
The looming Autumn Budget will be the first unveiled by Burnham's administration, with finance minister John Healey telling the Financial Times last month he wanted to carve out a fiscal "buffer against uncertainty."
Healey is tasked with bringing public spending and borrowing under control, with sticky inflation, elevated borrowing costs and lackluster economic growth adding to the urgency of balancing the books.
But Burnham and Healey have also said easing living costs, devolving political power to local authorities and raising defense spending remain priorities. While the government has identified some savings to help fund its defense plans, Burnham and Healey have yet to spell out the full mix of further savings or tax measures needed to pay for the additional expenditure while sticking to the U.K.'s so-called fiscal rules.
Burnham has refused to rule out tax hikes, and the British press is reporting that windfall taxes targeting banks might be on the table.
Lenders operating in the U.K. have lobbied against that proposal, with JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon meeting with Burnham and Healey in London last month.
In his interview with CNBC, Haldane warned against homing in on businesses in the budget.
"I think most would say that the great engine of growth is the private sector," he said. "[But] there's a real sense within the private sector that they are taxed out. A sense we're borrowing too much rather than too little, and therefore more of the same was not the route to growth, and I hope that's a penny that's beginning to drop inside government."
However, Haldane added that he thought the current government is "significantly underweight in its economic and financial expertise."
