articles.title: Wood Group offshore workers launch 48-hour strike in row over pay - BBC
articles.summary: Wood Group offshore workers launch 48-hour strike in row over pay  BBCStrikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies  The GuardianOil pipeline strike threatens UK fuel supplies  The TelegraphUnite escalates North Sea labor disputes at Apache and Wood Group  Offshore MagazineUnite backs strike at Apache and warns over Forties pipeline system  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Offshore workers on a number of North Sea platforms are taking strike action in a dispute over pay and conditions.
The Unite and RMT unions said they are in dispute with the Wood Group over its decision to "slash" the pay and conditions of dozens of offshore workers, including through the threat of issuing fire-and-rehire notices.
The strikes will affect a number of installations run by Harbour Energy, including the Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.
The Wood Group said it had been notified of the action and added that staff and operational safety remained its "top priority".
Production, instrument and mechanical technicians are among those set to walk out for a total of six days in October and November, beginning with a two-day walk-out which started at midnight.
Further walkouts are expected on 20 and 21 October and 3 and 4 November.
The RMT has also instructed its members not to work any overtime from 8 October until further notice.
The news comes after a warning that separate strike action by offshore workers at energy firm Apache could "severely disrupt" UK fuel supplies.
Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Unite will not allow the Wood Group to slash and burn our members' pay and conditions.
"This is a profitable company and it is despicable that it is threatening to fire and rehire its workers. This is corporate greed in its worst form."
Vic Fraser, Unite industrial officer, said: "Industrial action will inevitably impact the operation of Harbour Energy's offshore assets.
"The workforce has been left with no option but to strike against the Wood Group's threats and intimidation.
"Our members are saying enough is enough."
RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "Our members are not asking for special treatment or unreasonable improvements.
"They are standing up to defend the terms and conditions they already have.
"Strike action is always a last resort, but our members have clearly shown that they are prepared to stand together to defend their livelihoods and the terms and conditions they have worked under for many years.
"Furthermore, instead of working with the union to resolve these issues, the company has inflamed the situation by threatening the use of fire-and-rehire tactics."
A Wood Group spokesperson said: "We have received notification of planned industrial action involving union members employed by Wood on one of our Harbour Energy contracts.
"This is in relation to a recent consultation on changes to employment terms and conditions with employees.
"Personnel and operational safety remain our top priority."
A Harbour Energy spokesperson said: "We are aware of discussions between Wood and its employees and we hope a constructive resolution can be reached.
"Our priority remains the safety of our people and assets.
"We continue to work closely with all our contractors and expect to maintain safe and reliable operations and production across our business."

articles.title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor - BBC
articles.summary: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor  BBCUK ‘may no longer be investable’ if Jackdaw and Rosebank are blocked  The TimesUK risks ‘uninvestable’ reputation if North Sea projects are blocked, says energy boss  Financial TimesNorway oil giant warns UK investment at risk unless Rosebank approved  The TelegraphJackdaw and Rosebank refusal would mark ‘end of oil and gas production in UK’  The Scotsman
articles.full_text:
Oil giant Equinor has warned it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved.
"The question will be: is the UK investable in the future? I hope it will not come to that," said Anders Opedal, boss of the Norwegian state oil company which is part owner of the sites.
He told the BBC the company would "have to take a hard view about it" if a decision was made to reject new drilling.
The warning comes as the UK government is set to decide whether or not to grant final approval to extract oil and gas at Rosebank and Jackdaw, despite a ban pledged in Labour's election manifesto.
The government said any decision would take into account all relevant evidence.
'Political choice'
Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.
The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters.
Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade.
Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in".
He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas.
"It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it."
Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas.
Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said.
Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.
Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.
Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.
Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".
New drilling 'won't cut bills'
Tessa Khan, executive director of Uplift, an organisation that wants the UK to move away from fossil fuel production, said new drilling at Rosebank "won't cut our bills" and was a "bad deal for Britain".
"It's overwhelmingly oil for export – but it will make Equinor and its part-owner, the Norwegian government, richer, while Britain is left with high energy bills and a declining workforce."
Khan said Labour's "climate credibility is also on the line".
A government spokesperson said the North Sea remained a "vital national asset", adding that "oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis".
"Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo - BBC
articles.summary: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo  BBCNepal ends search and rescue after flood, focuses on rehabilitation  ReutersNepal ends flood search with over 5,000 still missing, including 189 Indians  The Times of IndiaUkraine appealed to Nepal over the disappearance of 56 Ukrainians following a flood • ANTIKOR portal  АНТИКОРNepal partially suspends search for over 5,200 missing after deadly floods  A...
articles.full_text:
At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month.
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites.
With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead.
Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati.
The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave.
"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says.
He has little doubt they are dead.
But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years.
Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month.
Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance.
Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death.
But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare.
"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari.
He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues.
For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate.
When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us.
Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them.
Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed.
Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data.
The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol.
The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over.
Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality.
Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue.
"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC.
He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to.
For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses.
The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households.
This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family.
The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster.
Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied.
"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities."
The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution.
In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required.
The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn).
At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy.
Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects.
Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders.
This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster.
For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar.
He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati.
But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village.
Once again, he is without a home.
"I have lost everything," he said.
So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal.
Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies.
He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home.
Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari

articles.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates - BBC
articles.summary: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates  BBCAirports to go contactless in major boost for UK passengers  GOV.UKThe five new air travel rules every British holidaymaker needs to know  The i PaperNew technology will see UK passengers able to pass through airport gates without showing passports  The IndependentFlying from France to UK? Your face will soon be your passport  The Connexion
articles.full_text:
Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced.
On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said.
The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically.
Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials.
If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer.
Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said.
Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country.
"By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security.
"Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families."
Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger".
She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout."
Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force.
"As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler.
"This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area."
Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted.

articles.title: BRIEFING ROOM: International trade and sanctions - Financier Worldwide
articles.summary: BRIEFING ROOM: International trade and sanctions  Financier Worldwide
articles.full_text:
November 2026 | BRIEFING ROOM | GLOBAL TRADE
Financier Worldwide Magazine
November 2026 Issue
FW discusses international trade and sanctions with Jan Dunin-Wasowicz at Bennink Dunin-Wasowicz, Patrick Murphy at Clyde & Co LLP, Adam M. Smith at Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP, and Daniel Martin at Holman Fenwick Willan.
FW: How would you characterise the recent evolution of the international trade and sanctions landscape? What do you see as the most significant risks, challenges and opportunities currently facing businesses?
Smith: The most significant challenge for global business from the evolution of sanctions and the most significant risks posed by these measures to global business have two things in common: they are both marked by unprecedented speed and diversity. How does a compliance-minded global firm keep up to date with rules and regulations that change on a nearly daily basis? In 2025, there were more than 100 material changes to US sanctions, sometimes more than one in a single day. This fluidity is exacerbated by the unprecedented diversity of measures imposed – including sanctions, export controls, import controls and tariffs – the agencies and jurisdictions promulgating these measures, and the risk assessments of counterparties. Indeed, counterparties’ risk appetites increasingly impose practical limitations on deals even if regulations may otherwise permit them.
Martin: Even Matt Damon’s Odysseus only had to contend with two insurmountable challenges, when tackling Scylla and Chrybdis. Legal and compliance professionals are currently dealing with three. First, the rate of change has never been greater, with new designations and other additions virtually daily. Second, sanctions programmes are increasingly divergent, with the US, European Union (EU) and UK following very different courses on Iran and Russia. And third, courts are now being asked to interpret the sanctions, resulting in ever greater complexity as they publish decisions on issues such as ownership and control, including looking through trust structures to the settlors. No wonder sanctions compliance feels like an endless journey, with deafening volume all around. Compliance professionals need to keep their eyes open to keep up with the constant change, and not plug their ears to the danger.
Dunin-Wasowicz: From an EU perspective, the international trade and sanctions landscape has evolved from a specialised area of regulatory compliance into a central element of the EU’s security policy. EU operators must now navigate a complex framework touching on financial sanctions, trade restrictions, export controls, investment screening and anti-circumvention measures at a time when the EU is becoming more assertive and the security environment is deteriorating. EU export controls are also increasingly considered through the broader lenses of economic security and competitiveness, particularly for advanced technologies. The challenge is that there are many moving parts and it is very difficult to plan ahead. The opportunity is to integrate sanctions and export control analysis into strategic decision making rather than treating it as a standalone compliance topic.
Murphy: The current landscape is slow tectonic drift, as the US, EU and UK pursue increasingly divergent policies. Sanctions coordination was arguably at its strongest between 2010 and 2018, when the US and EU worked to ensure that their respective regimes broadly targeted the same persons and activities, thereby limiting the most acute conflicts arising from overlapping extraterritorial obligations. Since then, however, the US has withdrawn from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the EU Blocking Regulation has regained practical significance, Brexit has produced a third autonomous sanctions regime, and the three principal Western sanctions powers have increasingly diverged in their political objectives. The consequences are evident. Designation lists no longer align, trade restrictions differ, as illustrated by the contrasting UK and EU approaches to Russian liquified natural gas, and multinational businesses must navigate increasingly complex and sometimes competing compliance obligations. China’s Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law (AFSL) adds a further layer of complexity for businesses with exposure to China.
FW: To what extent are sanctions now being used as active instruments of geopolitical pressure rather than traditional regulatory compliance tools?
Martin: Sanctions have always been instruments of geopolitical pressure, with commercial organisations caught in the crossfire. Three developments are worth noting. The first is that the rate of geopolitical change has increased exponentially, making it difficult for commercial organisations to anticipate and plan, given the risk that today’s policy position might be reversed tomorrow. Secondly, the impact on commercial organisations risks exceeding the impact on the individuals and regimes which are the true object of the sanctions. As the range of restrictions increases, and the balance of the targeted activities shifts from malign activities such as supplying military equipment to more ‘ordinary’ commercial activities, some argue that sanctions are not really a regulatory compliance tool. Instead, governments are threatening commercial organisations with criminal penalties and business terminating designations if they do not follow what are effectively geopolitical policy decisions. Thirdly, geopolitical instability is resulting in countersanctions being imposed, further increasing complexity.
Dunin-Wasowicz: Sanctions have always formed part of the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy, but their scale, complexity and strategic importance have increased markedly. Russia’s full-scale invasion was a turning point and added a strong security-related element to EU sanctions. Generally speaking, EU sanctions are used alongside export controls and other economic security instruments to restrict access to finance, services, technology and markets, and to constrain the capacity of targeted states and sectors. The measures against Russia illustrate this development. They extend beyond conventional asset freezes to banking, energy, transport, professional services, advanced technology and Russia’s military-industrial base. Sanctions are designed as instruments of pressure, but their effect depends on how rigorously operators implement them. Private sector compliance has, in that sense, become part of the policy mechanism itself. Businesses must therefore understand the geopolitical objectives while implementing complex rules in a challenging operational context.
Murphy: All sanctions – as distinct from generally applicable export controls – are instruments of geopolitical pressure. The UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office states expressly that sanctions are imposed to fulfil United Nations and other international obligations, advance foreign policy and national security objectives, and maintain international peace and security. Their political purpose is also apparent from the legislation itself. From the functional title of the EU regulation concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia’s actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine to the more emphatically named US legislation, the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act, the nomenclature makes clear that sanctions are overt tools of state policy.
Smith: Many of the world’s governments have started to deem almost any economic concern an issue of ‘national security’. Certain economic challenges, such as trade imbalances or technical issues about imports or exports, had once been handled within a traditional, technocratic regulatory framework. But now that economic security equals national security, all of these tools – sanctions, tariffs, export controls, foreign direct investment restrictions and others – have taken on an urgency, a violence and a presumed immunity from review that had once been reserved for a narrow band of issues that had imposed immediate physical security risks. A key element of this development has been the incorporation of an agile, war-fighting ethos into coercive economic actions, with the targeting of ever more economically consequential entities and jurisdictions and more creative uses of tools that aim to surgically apply pressure while calibrating on the fly as the situation on the ground changes. While this fluidity is a challenge to the private sector actors eager to comply, the speed and flexibility of the measures are so beneficial to global policymakers that it is unlikely they will give up this authority easily.
FW: How significant is the growing focus on third-country workarounds, intermediaries and indirect trading routes? What does this tell us about the changing nature of sanctions enforcement?
Dunin-Wasowicz: The focus on third-country workarounds is now central to EU sanctions policy. The EU increasingly addresses the risk that restricted goods, technology or services may reach Russia through distributors, transhipment points, newly created counterparties, or commercially unjustified ownership and payment structures. The twentieth package provides a concrete illustration: for the first time, the EU applied its anti-circumvention tool against a third country, Kyrgyzstan. This reflects a shift from formal counterparty screening toward examination of the transaction as a whole. EU operators are expected to consider the product, destination, end-user, routing, payment flow and commercial rationale, and to investigate relevant red flags. Enforcement is therefore increasingly concerned with whether the operator identified circumvention risks and responded proportionately, rather than merely whether the immediate customer appeared on a sanctions list. More generally, companies are evaluated not only on whether due diligence was performed, but also on how it was executed.
Smith: For as long as there have been sanctions,

articles.title: AfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time - BBC
articles.summary: AfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time  BBCState parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war  The GuardianThe AfD’s dominance in Saxony-Anhalt  The EconomistGerman far right secures first regional parliament president  Financial TimesGermany news: Far-right AfD gets first house speaker in a German state parliament  DW.com
articles.full_text:
A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.
Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".
Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties.
"The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.
This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment.
"We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.
The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community.
Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.
Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December.
His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events.
Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD.
Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD.
Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media.
Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature.
The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote.

articles.title: LS Power Gets $6 Billion for Largest Flagship Fund Amid AI Boom - Energy Connects
articles.summary: LS Power Gets $6 Billion for Largest Flagship Fund Amid AI Boom  Energy Connects
articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) LS Power, a privately-held developer and investor in power infrastructure in North America, has raised $6 billion for its flagship fund, its largest to date, amid a surge in electricity demand driven by artificial intelligence.
The vehicle, LS Power Equity Partners VI, exceeded its initial $4 billion target, according to a statement seen by Bloomberg News. The fund is larger than its predecessor, which raised $2.7 billion in 2024.
“It’s a capital-intensive business, and the opportunity set has never been bigger,” Darpan Kapadia, chief operating officer of Manhattan-based LS Power, said in an interview. “I think most of the capital we deploy will be into operating projects.”
Demand for the fund illustrates the current interest in megawatts as the US grid comes under strain from the growth in power needs and aging infrastructure. Existing power plants have become significantly more valuable because of supply chain constraints and the time needed to build new generation plants.
In January, the private equity developer sold a fleet of natural gas plants to publicly-traded power producer NRG Energy Inc. in a deal valued at $12 billion.
“Power demand is growing at rates that we haven’t seen for decades,” Kapadia said. He noted that data center demand can show up in 12 to 16 months whereas new supply could take more than five years, “so you have this mismatch.”
The fund will invest in natural gas-fired power, renewable energy sources, batteries, smaller energy resources dotting the grid and potentially in other critical energy infrastructure.
Nearly a third of the money raised has already been deployed, with about $1.7 billion going to the firm’s acquisition of natural gas-powered assets from Constellation Energy Corp. this past March. The investor has agreed to buy about $5 billion of US electric-generation assets in total from Constellation, as part of the mandated divestitures stemming from the US power company’s landmark acquisition of Calpine Corp.
Fund VI attracted commitments from pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds, asset managers, family offices and others, according to the statement. Altogether, six funds to date have raised about $13 billion of capital.

articles.title: Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Experts warn that Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command.
Russia is testing the limits of Europe's security without formally crossing into open war. Its attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent months, including strikes on civilian infrastructure. Russian drones entering NATO airspace have also become a recurring occurrence, while Western officials have raised the alarm over a rise in Moscow's hybrid operations across Europe.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport in early August. The incidents are raising a broader question: how far Moscow can escalate its pressure on European countries without prompting a direct military response.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with participants of the Ukraine Recovery Lab, sponsored by Erste Foundation and organized as part of the European Forum Alpbach in Austria, held Aug. 24-Sept 4.
What may look like a string of hybrid incidents increasingly resembles a sub-threshold war against Europe, says Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert.
The Everywhere War Tracker records a sustained campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, military provocations, and airspace violations, which has grown more intensive and audacious since 2024 as Moscow has tested how far it can push Europe without triggering open conflict.
"Russia is waging a war against the European model of freedom, equality, and solidarity, and against the institutions that sustain it, especially the EU. This is a war fought in small steps," says Leopold Schmertzing, а strategic foresight and security and defense policy expert.
"I struggle to see it ending without a fundamental change in either the current Russian model or the European one."
Schmertzing argues that, despite Europe contributing far more to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine than it did to earlier conflicts, most Europeans still experience it as a war happening somewhere else.
"My fear is that we will only fully wake up when our own capitals are attacked and our citizens are killed. By then, it will be too late to prepare," he added.
Experts believe Europe is better prepared for a potential confrontation with Russia than it was in 2022, but important gaps remain. Air defense, drones, communications, intelligence and joint command remain weak points, they say, while European militaries have yet to fully adapt to the realities of modern warfare.
Ukraine's experience shows that unmanned systems can have an outsized impact, but European defense spending has yet to reflect that lesson.
More than 80% of Russian targets destroyed on the battlefield are hit by drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in January.
"That is how the modern war looks like," says Kateryna Mykhalko, managing director of the German-Ukrainian defense industry consortium New Age Defense.
"At the same time, the technology delivering 80% of battlefield results receives only roughly 2% of European defense budgets," she adds.
The EU and Ukraine have sought to deepen cooperation in the sector. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance aims to accelerate the development and production of drones and counter-drone systems, combining Ukraine’s battlefield experience with Europe’s industrial capacity.
For Europe, the challenge is therefore twofold: closing military capability gaps while developing a response to forms of Russian aggression that experts believe are already unfolding across the continent.
"Russia is a hard nut to crack because it is deeply vulnerable in some respects and remarkably insulated in others," Schmertzing says. "We have a great deal to learn from Ukraine about where pressure works and where it doesn't."
Europeans need to pull their collective heads out of their arses.

articles.title: British Airways Overhauls First Class Service, Amenities, And Food: Game Changer Or Non-Story? - One Mile at a Time
articles.summary: British Airways Overhauls First Class Service, Amenities, And Food: Game Changer Or Non-Story?  One Mile at a TimeUp, up and a stay: BA claims renovated planes are like luxury hotels  The TimesBA wants to turn its A380 superjumbos into ‘luxury hotels in the sky’  The TelegraphBritish Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets  CNBCBritish Airways refurbishing A380s with ‘world’s largest’ business-class cabin  FlightGlo...
articles.full_text:
British Airways has made some great passenger experience announcements this week. The airline has announced plans to overhaul its lounges at London Heathrow Airport (LHR), and has also revealed the details of the all-new cabins coming to the Airbus A380s.
That’s not the only news, though. In addition to plans to introduce a new first class seat, the airline has also shared the details of its new first class soft product, which is coming to all planes, regardless of whether or not they have the new cabins.
British Airways is overhauling its first class soft product, with the first comprehensive changes that we’ve seen to the cabin since before the pandemic. Beyond the new seats, let’s take a look at what we can expect — all of these changes should be available effective immediately.
First, British Airways is introducing a new unisex first class cabin amenity kit from British heritage house Swaine. It’s available in two colors — royal blue and cream — and contains a selection of skincare products from Wildsmith, with a Circadian Rhythm collection, aimed at supporting hydration and comfort. Products include a face mist, hand and body lotion, ceramide multi-balm, lip balm, face cream, and an overnight mask.
Next, British Airways is introducing a new woven day blanket in first class, featuring a herringbone design. This is complemented by a navy blue cushion with subtle detailing. There’s also new cool-touch fabric navy sleepwear, along with slippers. Then with turndown service, the crew will prepare the bed with a lightweight cotton duvet and newly designed pillow.
When it comes to dining, British Airways is promising greater choice, with a new “From the Grill” concept, whereby customers can create their preferred meal from a selection of proteins, including British roast rack of lamb, grilled salmon, sides and sauces, as well as a selection of signature mains.
To go along with the new dining experience, the airline is rolling out contemporary stoneware and fine bone china. Cutlery is designed by Studio William, while wine glasses are developed in collaboration with Richard Brendon.
British Airways is also promising a new service standard in first class, with updated First Service Specialist (FSS) training, rolling out for all first class trained crews. This is “designed to enable a more personalised service,” and “the programme helps crew respond to individual preferences while delivering the warm, intuitive and attentive hospitality that defines First.”
It’s great to see British Airways overhauling its first class soft product. However, at least based on what we know so far, this strikes me as being ever so mildly evolutionary, rather than revolutionary. Admittedly British Airways isn’t providing many pictures or additional details about what has changed, but I just struggle to get overly excited about any of these changes.
Okay, there’s new cutlery, and new amenity kits, and first class flight attendants will be trained on… first class service. The customization of being able to create your own meal is nice, but also not exactly a game changer.
But look, it’s not like I was expecting British Airways to reinvent the wheel with its first class. When you look at transatlantic first class products, British Airways has three things going for it:
- The airline dominates slot controlled Heathrow, which has a lot of premium demand, and people value the ability to fly nonstop
- British Airways first class tends to be the most reasonably priced first class product across the Atlantic
- British Airways has a massive first class footprint, the second largest in the world (only after Emirates), so the airline has lots of first class seats to lots of destinations
When you look at the competitive dynamics, Air France La Premiere first class is much more of a niche product, and it’s priced at the top end of the market globally. It’s only available in select markets, and the cabin is small.
Meanwhile you have Lufthansa Allegris first class and SWISS Senses first class, which is almost a self-own in terms of the reduction in capacity it represents, as you have just three seats per plane, so they’re also trying to skim the market, though they seem to be struggling with figuring out how to price it correctly.
British Airways first class doesn’t need to be perfect, it just needs to be good enough. And I do think the airline is accomplishing that.
British Airways has just overhauled its first class soft product. While the airline is also introducing a new first class hard product, the new service, amenities, and food, are coming to all planes with British Airways first class.
There’s ultimately nothing here that’s revolutionary, but instead, we’re just talking about incremental improvements. First class flight attendants will be trained in first class service (wow!), there will be new pillows, blankets, amenity kits, cutlery and china, and even updates to dining, including the ability to increasingly customize meals.
This all seems like a logical evolution of the product. Is there anything here that should make anyone at Air France lose any sleep? Nope. But ultimately British Airways has a different strategy, and that’s fair enough.
What do you make of these British Airways updates?
The one time I flew BA (business) they ran out of water!!!, ice, and snacks. I was starving for the last two hours of a 10 hour flight because when one combines IAGs budgeting with D&O quality you end up with tapas portions…. Not eager to go back to IAG in any cabin.

articles.title: UAE, EU cut tariffs to boost trade to nearly $50 billion by 2032 - Khaleej Times
articles.summary: UAE, EU cut tariffs to boost trade to nearly $50 billion by 2032  Khaleej Times
articles.full_text:
A new trade corridor linking the UAE with five Eurasian markets has officially opened after the UAE-Eurasian Economic Union  Economic Partnership Agreement entered into force on Tuesday.
The agreement provides preferential market access between the UAE and the EAEU’s five member states Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Russia covering more than 86 per cent of tariff lines and about 96 per cent of the value of goods currently traded between the two sides.
Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.
The agreement is expected to help increase annual trade between the two markets to nearly $50 billion by 2032.
UAE-EAEU non-oil trade reached $33.6 billion in 2025, up 16 per cent from $29 billion in 2024 and more than four times its 2021 level.
Imports from EAEU countries stood at $17.8 billion last year, while UAE re-exports reached $13.7 billion. In the first half of 2026, bilateral non-oil trade rose a further 6.2 per cent year-on-year to $14.3 billion.
Faster trade, wider market access
The agreement reduces or eliminates customs duties on a broad range of products while simplifying trade procedures and addressing unnecessary barriers.
It also introduces rules covering customs cooperation, e-commerce, economic cooperation and the participation of small and medium-sized businesses in international trade.
Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, UAE Minister of Foreign Trade, said the agreement would turn growing trade momentum into practical opportunities for businesses.
“The entry into force of the UAE-EAEU Economic Partnership Agreement transforms strong commercial momentum into a practical platform for exporters, manufacturers and supply-chain partners,” he said.
“By improving market access, simplifying customs procedures and establishing clear, transparent rules, we are enabling businesses to move goods more efficiently and compete across a market spanning five important Eurasian economies.”
Al Zeyoudi said the agreement would also strengthen supply-chain resilience and food security, while creating opportunities in manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, automotive products, technology and precious metals.
Gateway to wider markets
For UAE exporters, it provides preferential access to the EAEU customs market, while businesses from the five member states can use the UAE as a gateway to markets across the Middle East, Africa and Asia.
The agreement forms part of the UAE’s wider trade strategy, which seeks to expand non-oil foreign trade and strengthen the country’s position as a global hub for trade and logistics.
The UAE’s Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement programme, launched in September 2021, has expanded the country’s network of trade partnerships across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas.
The latest agreement further strengthens the UAE’s push to build open, rules-based trade links with high-growth markets and support economic diversification.

articles.title: Global energy-mix remains “stubbornly carbon-intensive” - European Rubber Journal
articles.summary: Global energy-mix remains “stubbornly carbon-intensive”  European Rubber Journal
articles.full_text:
6 Oct 2026
Share:
Energy Institute: Renewables transition accelerating, but fossil still dominates
London – The global energy system is caught in a “troubling contradiction”: Renewable power is expanding rapidly, electrification is transforming transport, and battery storage is helping grids absorb cleaner electricity. Yet fossil fuels remain dominant, energy demand continues to grow, and emissions are still rising.
That’s according to Selene Law, head of the statistical review of world energy at the Energy Institute, reviewing the institute's '2026 Review of World Energy'* at a Cadence First Friday Club press briefing.
Global energy supply exceeded 600 exajoules, increasing by about 1.6%, as every major energy-source grew for a second consecutive year, Law set out at the event held 11 Sept in London.
Renewables, she noted, recorded the fastest ‘absolute growth’, but they were largely added to an expanding system rather than replacing fossil fuels.
Solar delivered the strongest performance, accounting for 71% of renewable-energy growth and increasing by 30% year-on-year.
“Falling panel prices have made solar one of the most competitive sources of new electricity. Economics is now driving adoption as powerfully as environmental policy,” explained the presenter.
Electricity demand, meanwhile, grew by around 3%, nearly twice the rate of total energy supply, Law commenting: “As vehicles, heating and industrial processes move towards electricity, the power sector is becoming central to decarbonisation.”
Leading this transformation in China, where electrification has also contributed to declining road-fuel demand – reportedly six times lower than in the US – including via advances in ‘electric heavy transport’.
Battery deployment is equally important, Law explaining that “grid-scale and behind-the-meter storage can balance variable solar and wind generation, reducing dependence on gas-fired power. “
The transition is consequently driving demand for critical minerals: annual lithium production has risen from a negligible level to about 292 kilotonnes over the past decade.
Carbon-intensive
However, law went on to describe the underlying energy-mix as remaining “stubbornly carbon-intensive”: Fossil fuels still provide around 86% of final energy supply, down just slightly from around 89% a decade ago. Natural gas alone supplies roughly a quarter of global energy demand.
Regionally, Europe has invested heavily in renewables and, particularly in France, nuclear power. The oil- and gas-rich Middle East has made less progress in diversifying its energy-mix. Developing countries face an additional barrier: limited access to affordable capital for clean infrastructure.
Law concluded with the “uncomfortable finding” that emissions increased again in 2025, adding that “renewable energy is making a difference, but rising demand is overwhelming its gains.”
Governments, she urged, “must therefore measure success by fossil-fuel displacement, not installations alone. Expanding transmission, scaling storage, electrifying transport and industry, and financing clean infrastructure in developing economies are essential.
“Until renewable energy delivers sustained declines in fossil-fuel consumption and emissions, the world will remain trapped between a cleaner future and a growing carbon-intensive present.”

articles.title: South Korea shipped fuel to Russia via sanctioned vessels, media reports - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: South Korea shipped fuel to Russia via sanctioned vessels, media reports  The Kyiv IndependentFuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on  The GuardianSouth Korea exports eased Russia fuel crisis caused by drone strikes, Ukraine says  ReutersSouth Korea shipped fuel to Russia on sanctioned tankers  TVP WorldRusso-Ukrainian war, day 1686: Sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
In several instances in July and August 2026, fuel was shipped from South Korea to Russia, according to the Guardian on Oct. 6.
Potentially undermining sanctions, over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, from South Korean ports were loaded onto sanctioned Russian tankers, the Guardian reported. The findings were based on an analysis of port records and ship-tracking data.
Seven Russian tankers, including three sanctioned by the UK and EU, made 14 voyages from the nation's far-eastern ports to South Korean ports, where they were loaded with fuel before returning. In one instance, fuel was loaded onto a Russian tanker via ship-to-ship transfer, avoiding South Korean ports.
The transfer of fuel does not appear to violate South Korean law, the Guardian reported, despite involving vessels sanctioned by Seoul's western partners. South Korean export controls against Russia currently focus on electronics, machinery, and vehicles.
While Moscow is known to use its shadow fleet of aging, poorly insured tankers to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure have sent it scrambling for fuel.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
On Oct. 4, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks.
Since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, South Korea has stood as an ally to Ukraine, sending 630 million euros ($706 million) in bilateral aid as of February 2026, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.
However, in recent weeks, relations between Seoul and Kyiv have been strained.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul after providing details of a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea during a Sept. 23 U.N. General Assembly speech. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Oct. 2 warned of "additional measures" against Ukraine if its government refuses to take responsibility for a downward spiral in Kyiv-Seoul relations.
While the South Korean foreign ministry did not comment on the findings directly, it told the Guardian in a statement that as “a responsible member of the international community, the [South Korean] government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”

articles.title: ECB’s Nagel: No clear ​signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: ECB’s Nagel: No clear ​signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
European Central Bank (ECB) policymaker and Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said in a speech in Sorrento, Italy during the European trading session on Monday that the impact of energy shock-driven inflation has yet not fed into wage growth.
Longer-term market-based and expert expectations remain consistent with the Eurosystem’s 2% inflation target.
Gas prices are especially vulnerable because storage levels are low.
Europe may need to buy substantially higher volumes during the winter.
The destruction of refining capacity is driving up prices for refined petroleum products significantly.
Drought, wildfires and fertiliser shortages also pose risks to food prices.
This was increasing the relative attractiveness of bonds among reserve asset managers.
The case for diversification into gold remains significant given continued geopolitical stress and the credit risk associated with high debt levels.
No immediate impact on the Euro (EUR) from ECB Nagel's comments. At press time, EUR/USD is down 0.3% to near 1.1215 even after recovering a majority of its early losses.
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.

The dialogue addressed market access terms covering over two billion people and a quarter of global gross domestic product, with India offering ninety-two point five per cent of tariff lines and the European Union opening ninety-seven per cent, encompassing more than ninety per cent of bilateral trade value. Participants reviewed challenges regarding weaponised tariffs, supply chain disruptions, trade imbalances with China, stalled negotiations with the United States, and the shift from multilateral institutions such as the World Trade Organization toward bilateral agreements. The session also evaluated India's bilateral investment treaty framework, clean energy transitions, small modular nuclear reactors, and the implications of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Crucial attention centred on maritime security risks across the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb, shipping insurance costs, fertilizer import expenses, agricultural safeguards, economic autonomy, and regulated migration and student mobility.

The petitions had sought the registration of First Information Reports and an investigation by a special investigation team into speeches linked to communal violence and protests. The bench dismissed the matters across two lists in a brief hearing, bringing an end to the proceedings that had been pending since 2020. A detailed written order is awaited.
A panel discussion addressed the strategic and economic significance of the European Union-India Free Trade Agreement amid global geopolitical shifts and trade weaponisation. Panellists noted that the trade pact aims to cut four billion euros in tariffs, offer the potential to double bilateral trade, and promote economic diversification and cooperation. The discussion examined transatlantic relations, United States trade pressures, subsidies from China, and the growing imperative for Europe to pursue strategic autonomy alongside increased defence spending. The conversation also highlighted the Indo-French strategic partnership between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Emmanuel Macron. Addressing negotiations, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman observed that India's procurement of Russian oil did not derail trade talks, noting the absence of legislative hurdles comparable to the US Lindsey Graham bill. She highlighted that the agreement will directly benefit India's labour-intensive export sectors—including textiles, footwear, toys, and small and medium enterprises—thereby boosting employment and expanding market access for women and Indian workers.
Speaking on trade negotiations and agreements, Union Minister Nirmala Sitharaman highlighted India's strategic approach to bilateral trade pacts while navigating global trade pressures. Addressing discussions surrounding the proposed India-EU trade pact, termed the mother of all deals, Sitharaman noted that the agreement covers two billion people and a quarter of global GDP, with both sides opening more than 90% of tariff lines and value while safeguarding sensitive agricultural sectors. Remarking on broader global tensions, she stated that 'tariff has become weaponised' instead of serving merely as an instrument of negotiation within established frameworks. Regarding ongoing talks with the United States, Sitharaman pointed out that negotiations remain rigorous, with both sides navigating an existing trade balance that is in India's favour. She also highlighted the exponentially growing trade imbalance with China since 2014, emphasising that despite severe discrepancies, resolving trade imbalances ultimately requires structured negotiation and mutual give-and-take rather than unilateral weaponisation of tariffs.

articles.title: India-US Trade Talks Hit ‘Plateau’; Russian Oil Did Not Dictate EU Deal: Sitharaman - Open Magazine
articles.summary: India-US Trade Talks Hit ‘Plateau’; Russian Oil Did Not Dictate EU Deal: Sitharaman  Open Magazine
articles.full_text:
India-US trade negotiations have reached a “plateau” where further concessions could prove difficult for either side, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said, even as she maintained that talks were continuing.
Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, Sitharaman also said India’s purchases of Russian oil had not been a determining condition in trade negotiations with the European Union. Her remarks outlined the challenge facing Indian negotiators: securing greater market access while protecting domestic interests and preserving strategic autonomy.
LIMITED ROOM FOR GIVE AND TAKE
Sitharaman said negotiations with Washington remained intensive, but suggested that the scope for further compromise had narrowed.
“The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” she said.
The minister identified India’s trade surplus with the US as a central issue in the relationship, acknowledging that Washington would seek to narrow the imbalance.
“But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor,” she said.
Sitharaman also pointed to changes in how countries pursued trade disputes and concessions. Tariffs, traditionally an instrument used within a negotiating framework, had become part of a more unsettled trading environment. Countries nevertheless needed to continue negotiating and find room for “some give and take”, she said.
‘NO LINDSEY GRAHAM BILL’ IN EUROPE
Asked whether India’s procurement of Russian oil had become a sticking point with European partners, Sitharaman said it had not determined the course of negotiations.
“In Europe, as much as I understand till today, there is no Lindsey Graham bill,” she said.
“I don't think there was a card on the table saying hey this is going to determine what we do next in the negotiation.”
The minister acknowledged that a range of issues came up in formal and informal discussions surrounding trade talks, while distinguishing those exchanges from conditions governing an agreement.
EU MARKET ACCESS, WITH DOMESTIC SAFEGUARDS
Sitharaman presented the India-EU agreement as an example of expanding trade while retaining protection for sensitive sectors, particularly agriculture.
India had opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines and around 97 per cent of trade value, she said. The EU’s opening covered 99 per cent in value terms and, she indicated, approximately 97 per cent of tariff lines.
Greater access to European markets could benefit labour-intensive industries such as footwear, textiles, toys and processed products, many of which involve micro, small and medium enterprises.
“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labor-intensive,” Sitharaman said, adding that expanded access could bring “more exports, more jobs”.
BILATERAL DEALS GAIN GROUND
The finance minister linked India’s pursuit of bilateral agreements to weakening multilateral institutions and disruptions in global supply chains.
“Now the balance is somewhat tilted in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she said.
Countries were seeking new partners and using trade agreements to strengthen those relationships, with greater attention to keeping supply chains functioning. Bilateral and multilateral arrangements, she stressed, were never mutually exclusive.
“Multilateralism is not going to go away and multilateralism shouldn't go away,” Sitharaman said.
With inputs from ANI

articles.title: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times, documents reveal - BBC
articles.summary: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times, documents reveal  BBCUK's Stanlow refinery under fresh investigation for pollution, spills  Quantum Commodity IntelligenceStanlow refinery broke permit conditions 58 times in two years, Environment Agency finds |  Deeside.comOil refinery accused of hundreds of major pollution spills  Energy Live NewsUK’s Stanlow oil refinery refinery breached pollution limits 58 times  en.bd-pratidin.c...
articles.full_text:
- Published
One of the UK's biggest oil refineries spilled pollution into local rivers and the Mersey Estuary on dozens of occasions in 2023 and 2024, documents shared exclusively with the BBC suggest.
EET Fuels, formerly known as Essar, which runs Stanlow refinery, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law between 2018 and 2020.
But documents obtained by investigative journalists from SourceMaterial describe other breaches from the refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, with toxic chemicals and oil regularly spilled into the waterways and even groundwater.
EET Fuels said it "takes its environmental responsibilities extremely seriously".
The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed that it is investigating the breaches.
The Stanlow oil refinery is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK and processes 10 million tonnes of crude oil each year - producing around 18% of the country's fuel for road transport like cars and trucks.
EET Fuels, which bought the refinery from Shell in 2011 for £842m, holds a permit to operate the site.
This says it can discharge controlled amounts of oil and chemicals into the air and waterways. However, it must make efforts to limit pollution to the environment and harm to humans.
But reports from the EA into activities at the refinery, uncovered by environmental journalists SourceMaterial, show that in 2023 and 2024 the permitted levels for chemical releases were exceeded hundreds of times.
The regulator has determined this meant EET Fuels broke its permit conditions 58 times over the two-year period - which could amount to an offence.
The documents show the spills included toxic chemicals such as cyanide, benzene, and heavy oils - into the air and local waterways like Thornton Brook and the River Gowy which connect onto the River Mersey Estuary.
The estuary is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and home to endangered species including dolphins and a breeding ground for rare birds.
"Species like dunlin, black-tailed godwit and redshank will travel all around the world to feed and roost in the land around the River Mersey," explained Charlotte Harris, chief executive of Cheshire Wildlife Trust.
Harris said this has only been possible because organisations, including the Wildlife Trusts, have undertaken years of pollution clean up from legacy industry in the area.
"We've seen the Atlantic salmon return to the river and also the critically endangered European eel makes its way up the Mersey and into the River Gowy to breed each year as well," she said.
EA documents detail how pollutants like sulphur dioxide were released into the air at seven times permitted levels, cyanide into waterways like the Gowy at more than eight times permitted levels, and oil at more than thirteen times the allowed levels.
In one incident in July 2023, the company breached its permit after rainwater containing oil leaked from the site - the EA classed the event as "significant".
In its report it said there were a "significant number" of complaints from locals about the smell and further investigations indicated the oil had contaminated groundwater supplies.
EET Fuels told the BBC that the oil lost was on a "low scale" and "was strictly localised to two boreholes, all well within the Stanlow site itself".
A year later on 12 September 2024, another EA report says that oil was spilled again from the site. More than a tonne of oil was released into Thornton Brook and spread to the Mersey Estuary.
EET Fuels reported the incident to the authorities, but it took nearly two weeks for the company to provide an estimate of how much oil was spilled - another breach of the regulations which requires this within 24 hours.
An emergency response team was organised including regulators the EA and Natural England, local port authorities and the Fisheries Authority - according to meeting documents.
Natural England (NE), which regulates SSSIs, said in one meeting: "What has gone in there is going to have some impact on the vegetation and salt marsh and there is probably still a risk of ingestion by birds."
A drone was sent up to survey the scale of the damage which revealed oil had spread for more than a mile down the river and "there was brown discolouration around the reedbed". The footage showed wading birds - including the red-listed Dunlin - in the area.
"Where we have chemical pollution the impact isn't just localised. When it enters the river system, that system is highly dynamic and high energy, which means that pollution spreads far and wide really, really quickly," said Harris.
A floating barrier was deployed to try and contain the spill.
The regulators decided that because the site was not easily reachable, the public health risk was low, but a decision was made to close local cockle beds in the estuary while the water quality was tested by the Food Standards Agency (FSA).
The beds were given the all clear, but were closed for five weeks whilst testing took place.
Mark Taylor, CEO of the Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority North West, told the BBC: "The incident led to a delay in the fishers being able to derive an income from the bed".
He added that they were able to make up this income later in the season.
The incident was later categorised by the EA as a "minor" breach of the company's permit.
EET Fuels told the BBC in a statement: "Selectively chosen, historical permit exceedances from prior years in no way represent the current operational status, improving environmental performance, or governance of the refinery today."
The Environment Agency has launched a separate criminal investigation into what happened in September 2024 and told the BBC it remained "ongoing".
It said it was yet to confirm what action to take in relation to the 2023 offences.
Regulator drops investigation
As well as the Environment Agency's investigation, Natural England began its own investigation after the 2024 incident.
It eventually dropped this, and told the BBC: "Our assessment found that, while it was regrettable that the incident occurred, the environmental impact on the SSSI was minor."
But in internal emails Natural England told the EA its reason for dropping the investigation was it thought the company's permit to operate did not set any limits for how much oil could be released - despite the pollution risks.
Its officers wrote: "Thank you for sending the permit…. which verify Stanlow's stance that the storm overflow is permitted and further with no limit set to the quantity of oil released. With this in place, Natural England have decided not to take any further action."
James Wallace, chief executive at charity River Action, said these documents suggest "we're seeing a downgrading of pollution incident[s]... where evidence is being ignored."
When asked about its reasons for dropping the investigation, Natural England said its role was to assess the impact on the protected site and that any questions about "compliance with the environmental permit are matters for the Environment Agency".
Environmentalists urge swifter action
EET Fuels is due to be sentenced next month for the previous permit breaches between 2018 and 2020.
Wallace said the fact this case took up to eight years to reach the courts and the company appears to have breached environmental law repeatedly, calls into question the effectiveness of the regulators in deterring environmental pollution.
"We need to see consistent law enforcement, and we need to see the threat of punitive measures by all industries, whether it's the water industry or oil refineries," Wallace said.
Harris from Cheshire Wildlife Trust agreed the current regulations were "not solving the problem at source at the moment".
"So when a business does impact a river like this, it is absolutely vital that they're held to account. But going further than that, it shouldn't be happening in the first place. We really do need to get a grip of how we treat our river systems," she added.
EET Fuels, also told the BBC: "[It] has backed its environmental commitments with decisive action, investing over £24 million in major wastewater infrastructure alone and delivering a measurable, upward trend in Environment Agency compliance ratings, improving from an F rating in 2023 to an E rating in 2024 as major capital projects came online."

articles.title: A Message from The Elders - em24.uk
articles.summary: A Message from The Elders  em24.uk
articles.full_text:
Dear friends,
The climate crisis will not wait for the world’s geopolitics to improve. As leaders gather for COP31 in Turkey next month, half-measures are no longer enough. They must arrive with the courage to act, not just statements to describe the situation. And they must leave Antalya with commitments equal to the scale of the crises we are already experiencing: record heatwaves, devastating floods, and a major energy-security shock created by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The pressures are only mounting. A Super El Niño – exacerbated by climate change – now threatens to increase the risks of drought, extreme heat, floods and storms across the globe. The additional heat alone is projected to cause 450,000 more deaths worldwide. As world leaders prepare for COP31 in Turkey next month, they must have the tenacity and vision to work together to tackle the challenge head on.
There must be clear leadership from the COP Presidencies of Australia and Turkey. They must mobilise countries behind a clear and credible plan for tangible progress. As Elders, we are clear on the direction of travel: this is the moment to accelerate the just transition away from fossil fuels and towards clean energy, decisively.
The answer to the twin challenges we face – extreme weather and energy security – cannot be to double down on the energy sources that have left us exposed. Instead, we must accelerate the global transition to secure, affordable and clean energy. France and Germany have set the ball rolling – both publishing national roadmaps with timelines for phasing out the use of coal, oil and gas. We must see more countries following in their footsteps.
Throughout my career in public service, I have argued that the way to secure our common future is through solidarity and collective action. These principles are more vital now than ever. Promisingly, we have seen two coalitions emerge over the course of this year: the Santa Marta initiative, focused on accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels, and Electrify Now, focused on expanding electrification. COP31 offers a key moment to build on this good momentum and for countries, cities and companies to find fresh opportunities for collaboration.
Another area where more progress needs to be made is that of climate finance, which moves far slower than the pace of the climate crisis. It is often those who have contributed the least to global emissions that are now suffering the most. As the world tips over the 1.5 degrees threshold, no community should be left to face a climate disaster without adequate protection.
Those who have had the greatest hand in causing the climate crisis must not shirk their responsibilities. Developed countries must lead in delivering the promised climate finance to help people adapt and respond to climate extremes.
I hope that Turkey and Australia can rally countries at COP31 to respond with greater action and practical partnerships. As extreme weather events and high energy prices are set to continue, the world will be watching.
With thanks for your ongoing support,
Gro Harlem Brundtland
06/10/2026
