articles.title: What’s driving Europe’s battery boom? Insights from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey and Storage Report - pv magazine Global
articles.summary: What’s driving Europe’s battery boom? Insights from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey and Storage Report  pv magazine Global
articles.full_text:
Europe’s battery storage market is entering a new phase as utility-scale projects become the industry’s main growth engine, creating fresh opportunities for manufacturers while reshaping competition across residential and commercial markets. According to EUPD Research’s new calculations, Europe’s (EU + UK + Switzerland + Norway + Ukraine) annual battery storage installations are projected to increase from 34 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025 to 65 GWh in 2026, marking one of the region’s fastest periods of market expansion.
The shift reflects more than stronger battery demand. Higher electricity prices, tighter energy markets, expanding renewable generation and supportive policy measures are changing storage from a complementary technology into an increasingly important part of Europe’s electricity system. Rather than serving only as a backup solution for homes and businesses, batteries are becoming a critical tool for balancing power systems as solar and wind account for a larger share of electricity generation.
Recent findings from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey, indicate buoyant demand sentiment across major European markets. The survey gathered responses from a broad base of installation companies, providing a representative view of current market sentiment.
Figure 1: Solar & Storage Demand Across Major European Markets
Utility-Scale Projects Drive the Next Wave of Growth
The strongest momentum is emerging in large-scale battery projects connected directly to the grid. EUPD Research expects the utility segment alone to install a record of around 44 GWh of storage in 2026, making it the largest contributor to Europe’s overall market growth.
Countries with rapidly expanding renewable fleets are leading that transition as grid operators increasingly rely on batteries to shift electricity across different hours of the day, improve system flexibility and support network stability. While electricity prices have eased from the extraordinary peaks seen during Europe’s energy crisis, they remain high enough in many markets to strengthen the business case for storage investments.
Policy is reinforcing that trend. European electricity market reforms, funding mechanisms, permitting improvements and national storage support measures are creating a more favorable environment for deployment, particularly for larger projects that help integrate growing volumes of renewable electricity. At the same time, changing incentive structures in several countries are encouraging households and businesses to maximize self-consumption, making batteries more attractive as export payments for rooftop solar decline or net-metering schemes begin to phase out.
Bigger Projects Reshape the Competitive Landscape
The expansion of utility-scale storage is changing how manufacturers participate in Europe’s battery storage market. As projects become larger and more complex, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies are becoming increasingly specialized, creating a more structured project ecosystem than the fragmented market that characterized earlier stages of deployment.
Insights from the newly released EUPD PV and Storage C&I EPCMonitor© 2026 indicate that local contractors continue serving smaller installations, while national leaders, regional players and pan-European firms are taking on progressively larger battery projects across multiple countries. That differentiation is creating multiple routes to market for manufacturers, allowing suppliers to build longer-term partnerships with contractors that specialize in infrastructure-scale delivery instead of relying primarily on equipment sales.
Project size is increasingly defining competitive positioning. Companies focused on smaller systems continue serving distributed markets, while firms capable of delivering larger projects are becoming more important as utilities, developers and industrial customers pursue higher-capacity installations. The result is a market where partnerships and delivery capabilities are becoming as important as battery technology itself.
Figure 2: Annual Installed EES Capacity | Company Type | 2025
Residential Storage Enters a More Competitive Phase
While utility-scale deployment is accelerating, distributed storage is entering a more mature stage rather than slowing. Europe’s residential market is becoming increasingly sophisticated as manufacturers expand beyond standalone batteries into broader home-energy ecosystems that combine rooftop solar, electric vehicle charging, heat pumps, energy management software and grid-flexibility services.
Several market forces continue supporting residential adoption. High retail electricity prices, declining battery costs, tax incentives, value-added tax (VAT) exemptions and growing interest in energy independence remain important drivers across Europe. However, the market also faces persistent challenges, including uneven smart-meter deployment, financing constraints, labor shortages and the gradual reduction of some subsidy programs in certain countries.
Despite those headwinds, EUPD Research expects Europe to install roughly 15 GWh of new residential battery capacity during 2026, with Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and the United Kingdom remaining among the strongest-performing markets.
According to EUPD Research’s latest EES Report Europe© H1 2026, the competitive landscape is evolving just as quickly as deployment. Residential supplier rankings have already shifted between 2025 and the first half of 2026, illustrating how rapidly manufacturers are competing for market share as customer preferences change. Germany’s residential storage market is becoming increasingly fragmented, as share gradually shifts away from the leading suppliers. The top suppliers’ combined share declined between 2025 and H1 2026, while mid-sized brands and smaller brands expanded their presence. These trends point to a market where competition is intensifying and leadership positions are becoming less secure.
Figure 3: Germany’s Residential Storage Supplier Landscape: 2025 Vs H1 2026
Instead of competing only on battery hardware, manufacturers are increasingly differentiating themselves through integrated energy solutions, software capabilities and broader customer offerings that create additional value after installation.
Storage Becomes Core Energy Infrastructure
Europe’s battery market is increasingly developing along two complementary paths rather than replacing one segment with another. Utility-scale batteries are becoming essential infrastructure for balancing renewable electricity and supporting grid operations, while distributed storage is expanding its role within homes and businesses through integrated energy-management systems.
For manufacturers, this creates a dual opportunity. Larger grid-connected projects provide access to infrastructure-scale investment, while distributed markets offer opportunities to deepen customer relationships through broader energy solutions and connected technologies. As Europe moves toward a projected 65 GWh storage market in 2026, batteries are becoming less of a standalone clean-energy product and more of a core component of the region’s evolving electricity system.
The next phase of this market will be shaped not only by how many batteries are installed, but also by how effectively storage becomes embedded across both the power grid and the wider energy ecosystem. Partnerships and delivery capabilities will become increasingly important, particularly in the commercial and industrial segment, where solar, storage and energy management are converging into a single business case.
This is where industry collaboration becomes critical. European Sustainability Week 2026, taking place from 23 to 25 November at the historic Petersberg near Bonn, brings together manufacturers, EPCs, utilities, investors and industrial energy buyers to explore these developments. As Europe’s C&I event for sustainable industries, with a clear focus on renewable energy, solar and storage, it provides a platform for the exchange of market insights and practical solutions. At the Environmental Forum on 24 November, EUPD Research will share the latest market insights, while industry leaders will discuss how storage can become core infrastructure for European businesses.
Last year, more than 600 decision-makers from over 23 countries took part. Registration is open at european-sustainability-week.com.
Authors: Daniel Fuchs and Ali Arfa
Daniel Fuchs is the Chief Customer Officer of EUPD Group. He has extensive international experience in sales, marketing, customer engagement, and strategic event management within the renewable energy and cleantech industries. His work focuses on building customer-centric growth strategies, strengthening global partnerships, and supporting market development across the solar, energy storage, and sustainability sectors. He can be reached atd.fuchs@eupd-research.com.
Ali Arfa is the Head of Data Management at EUPD Research. He is a graduate of the University of Bonn and with a background in European and North American politics. His expertise encompasses market research, policy development, and stakeholder analysis. His particular focus is on solar energy, energy storage, and strategic consultation. articles.summary: UK events firm that hosts arms fairs and comic shows sold to rival for £2bn  The GuardianInforma to Separate Academic Business; Buys Clarion Events for $2.96 Billion  WSJInforma to buy rival events business Clarion from Blackstone for £2.2bn  Financial TimesInforma to acquire Clarion from Blackstone in £2.24bn deal, and to spin off academic arm  Exhibition NewsUK's FTSE 100 Extends Gains; Informa Rises on Clarion Deal  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
A British events business that hosts arms fairs and conventions for comic book fans has been snapped up by a FTSE 100 rival for more than £2bn.
Informa has struck a £2.24bn deal to buy the London-based events organiser Clarion from the private equity group Blackstone
The takeover will add more than 100 events to Informa’s portfolio – from the defence and security exhibit DSEI held at London’s ExCel, to the comic book and pop culture themed Awesome Con in Washington.
DSEI, which is held every two years in London as well as in Germany and Japan, has also attracted protests.
Last year, hundreds demonstrated outside the four-day fair in London in protest against Israel’s three biggest arms companies present at the event. Elbit Systems, Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries have supplied the Israel Defense Forces; the latter two are state-owned.
Clarion’s portfolio also spans travel shows, classic car meet-ups and events for the technology, gaming, design and technology industries. Its Classic Motor Show event in Birmingham next month is billed as the “world’s largest vehicle club gathering”.
Stephen Carter, the Informa chief executive, said the company was “accelerating the focus” on its core live events business, as it also laid out plans to spin off its academic publishing arm, Taylor & Francis.
Informa, which is headquartered in London and employs 14,000 people, hosts big industry events around the world, including London Tech Week and the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity.
However the FTSE 100 group’s shares have been flat so far this year as it was forced to reschedule several events in the Middle East because of the conflict in the region.
Last year Carter, who has led the group since 2013, moved his residency from the UK to the UAE and retired from the House of Lords. Informa makes more than a third of its revenue in India, the Middle East and Asia.
The academic publishing business made about $1bn (£760m) last year. Informa said that it had launched a formal process to separate Taylor & Francis, and that it would “review all options”. The outcome of the review will be reported alongside its full-year results in March next year.
Taylor & Francis, which was founded in London in 1852, joined Informa in 2004. It publishes journals and books about science, medicine, technology and engineering.
Informa told investors on Tuesday that in order to fund the Clarion deal, it will raise £940m through a share placing, which will include an offer for armchair investors through the broker RetailBook.
The takeover is expected to accelerate Informa’s growth and bolster its earnings per share from 2027, the company said. Shares in the business, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, rose by 1.4% in early trading on Tuesday.

articles.summary: ECB’s Rehn: High long-term rates contributing to a slowdown in growth  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The comments from European Central Bank (ECB) official and Finnish Central Bank Governor Olli Rehn released during the European trading session on Tuesday signal economic warnings due to higher long-term interest rates.
Comments
High long-term rates contributing to a slowdown in growth and reduces pass-through of energy prices to other prices and to wages.
We have not seen inflation spread to non-energy prices or wages.
Market Reaction
There seems to be no impact of ECB Rehn's comments on the Euro (EUR). At press time, EUR/USD trades 0.12% higher to near 1.1233 due to some correction in the US Dollar (USD).
ECB FAQs
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.
Author
Sagar Dua is associated with the financial markets from his college days. Along with pursuing post-graduation in Commerce in 2014, he started his markets training with chart analysis.

articles.title: Turkey and Pakistan to send troops to Saudi Arabia under defence pact - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Turkey and Pakistan to send troops to Saudi Arabia under defence pact  Euronews.comSaudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey trigger mutual defence pact  Financial TimesPakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means  Al JazeeraMecca Pact and Türkiye’s flexible deterrence  Daily SabahTurkey and Pakistan pledge to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia  Le Monde.fr
articles.full_text:
The three signatories of the August Mecca Joint Defence Agreement met in emergency session in Riyadh and agreed to move immediately to "rapid deployment" of military forces, uniting NATO's second-largest army, the Islamic world's only nuclear state and the largest Gulf power.
Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a "rapid deployment" of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said Monday, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen's Houthis.
In August, the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing to come to each other's aid if one were attacked.
The pact unites NATO's second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world's only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the largest Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Tehran-backed Houthis by name.
The trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom's security and territorial integrity", they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed "to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom".
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which on Monday launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh's support, seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade.

articles.title: Musabegovic: euribor to rise again, what it means for loans - srpske.rs
articles.summary: Musabegovic: euribor to rise again, what it means for loans  srpske.rs
articles.full_text:
Consumer prices in the eurozone were 3.8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, the highest rate in three years and above expectations, Bloomberg Adria reports. The European Central Bank’s target is two percent. Ismail Musabegovic, a professor at the Belgrade Banking Academy, said on the RTS Morning Program on October 6 that he expects another rise in euribor, and with it higher payments on euro-linked loans.
In Serbia, according to RTS, inflation in recent months has stayed below the midpoint of the National Bank of Serbia’s target. For that reason Musabegovic expects neither a significant rise in domestic inflation nor a heavy blow to household budgets from loans.
Why energy pushes interest rates up
Musabegovic names energy prices as the cause. In his words, prices are being driven by the conflict between the United States and Iran and by the war in Ukraine, and if the warring sides reached a deal, inflationary pressure would ease, mainly because of damaged energy facilities and the closed Strait of Hormuz. The price of gas, he says, has passed 720 dollars per thousand cubic meters.
“The global economic challenges are incredible. In essence, the problem is energy, which is pushing inflation up to the point where central banks in Europe have to run a restrictive monetary policy. The euro is used as a means of payment by 21 countries, so the decisions of the European Central Bank are within their remit.”
The professor describes the consequence for the price of money this way:
“At this moment the room for cheap money is closed, and it will not be there any time soon. Monetary policy is getting stricter and more restrictive, so money has become more expensive in order to curb inflation.”
He is not optimistic about winter. “Everyone is struggling to secure reserves for the winter, but I am not optimistic that the situation will improve,” Musabegovic said of gas stocks.
What he expects from euribor and loan payments
Euribor is the interest rate at which European banks lend to one another, and mortgage contracts are built on the three-month or six-month version. Musabegovic gave his expectation, but not an estimate of the size of the jump:
“As for euribor, I think there will be another increase. Whether it will be 0.25 percentage points, that will be felt by people who have housing loans indexed to the euro.”
How often a borrower feels the change depends on the contract. With three-month euribor the payment is adjusted four times a year, with six-month euribor twice.
“If you have a variable interest rate that adjusts every three months, your payment will change four times a year, while with six-month euribor the payment changes twice a year. When you are at the start of repaying a loan, you may feel the biggest increase in the payment, unlike when you are in the middle or at the end of repayment.”
How much has euribor already risen?
Euribor figures need to be read by maturity, because they do not refer to the same indicator. Biznis i finansije, citing Euronews Srbija, reports that the one-month euribor rose from about 2.1 percent at the start of the year to almost three percent by September 22, with a sharp climb during September. The three-month and six-month rates have each risen by about 30 percent since January. Srbija Danas reported on October 4 that the six-month euribor passed three percent for the first time this year.
Professor Zoran Grubisic of the same academy told Euronews Srbija: “This is a classic energy shock, the kind we last had in 2022 and 2023.” Oil, he says, is holding steadily above 100 dollars a barrel. In that conversation he said another increase is signaled before the end of the year, but that he does not expect new large increases in the European Central Bank’s benchmark rates:
“I think there will be no further hikes from the European Central Bank, and then euribor has no reason to react to those expectations either.”
What protects borrowers
Both Musabegovic and Grubisic point to legal protection. Musabegovic does not expect the National Bank of Serbia to raise its benchmark rate, and explains why borrowers with euribor-linked loans are shielded:
“A change in the benchmark interest rate in Europe could lead the National Bank of Serbia to consider a possible increase, but personally I do not expect that to happen, because everyone who has loans indexed to euribor is protected by law, and caps have been introduced up to which banks can raise interest rates.”
The rule is easy to misread. According to Srbija Danas, and as Darko Stamenkovic, head of the National Bank of Serbia’s Banking Supervision Department, also explained, for 2026 and 2027 the maximum interest rate on housing loans is set as the weighted average interest rate plus one fifth, that is, 20 percent. That is an upper limit on the level of the interest rate, not a rule that a payment may rise by at most 20 percent. The actual change in a monthly obligation depends on the loan and on how the payment is calculated. The central bank, it is reported, says that no dramatic changes are expected.
Grubisic argues that the increase is already priced into the legal cap: “Even if euribor keeps rising, their combined interest rate cannot go up, because that is, after all, protected by law.”
Governor Jorgovanka Tabakovic spoke about the National Bank of Serbia’s earlier measure, and Srbija Danas carries her statement:
“We capped interest rates in 2023 and the payments on the covered loans were reduced by 10 to more than 25 percent. The average interest rate on new housing loans was lowered from 6.4 percent in September 2023 to 4.5 percent in June 2026. On a loan whose payment was 518 euros, that is 76 euros less every month.”
By that example the monthly obligation fell from 518 to 442 euros, or 912 euros a year.
Is it time to refinance?
Grubisic does not advise rushing. Housing loans run for 20 or 25 years, so precise projections are hard, he says, and he would not decide to switch to a fixed rate “based on events that happen from time to time.” A fixed rate is not bad in itself, but:
“I would not chase refinancing now. Those ‘curves’ usually cost you more.”
What a euribor rise will mean for an individual borrower depends on the contract: whether it is tied to three-month or six-month euribor, when the rate is adjusted, and how long remains until the loan is repaid. We wrote on October 3 about citizens’ total debt to banks, which stood at 2,187 billion dinars in September. This story is about the price of that debt.

articles.title: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights - Spherical Insights
articles.summary: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
Italy is backing Silicon Box to strengthen semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech investment, create jobs, reduce supply-chain vulnerabilities and establish Italy as a strategic European hub for advanced digital manufacturing.
Italy has cleared the financing framework for Silicon Box’s planned semiconductor manufacturing facility in Novara, marking a major step in the country’s strategy to strengthen its position in Europe’s semiconductor industry. The project, known as the Vulcan Project, involves a total investment of €3.2 billion, equivalent to roughly $3.7 billion, with the Italian government providing €1.3 billion (US$1.45 billion) in public support through the semiconductor sector fund established under the European Chips Act.
The project will establish Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing facility and is expected to focus on the back-end stages of semiconductor production, particularly chiplet integration, advanced packaging and testing. According to Italy’s Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, the Novara facility would be the first of its kind in Europe, introducing advanced chiplet and packaging capabilities that are currently not available at this scale within the European Union.

A strategic investment in semiconductor manufacturing
The Silicon Box investment in Novara, Italy, represents a €3.2 billion strategic project aimed at strengthening Europe’s semiconductor supply chain. In October 2026, Italy’s investment agency Invitalia approved €1.3 billion in public support, equivalent to roughly 41% of the total investment. The facility is expected to become Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing site and is projected to create around 1,600 direct jobs at full capacity.
The project focuses on advanced chiplet integration, packaging and testing, technologies increasingly important for artificial intelligence, data centres, electric and autonomous vehicles, telecommunications and high-performance computing. The European Commission granted the facility Open EU Foundry status in March 2026, with full production capacity expected by 2033.
For Italy, the investment supports a broader semiconductor strategy. The country has a multibillion-euro Chips Fund, more than €1 billion committed to EU microelectronics IPCEI projects, and a €225 million (US$252 billion) semiconductor-design centre in Pavia. Italy also ranks second in the EU by number of companies in electronic components and boards.
The project aligns with the EU Chips Act, which aims to mobilise over €100 billion (US$112.1 billion) in policy-driven investment and raise Europe’s semiconductor market share from about 10% to 20% by 2030.
Focus on advanced packaging and chiplets
Silicon Box’s Novara project is significant because it targets the “back-end” of semiconductor production, an area increasingly important as conventional chip scaling becomes more difficult. Instead of producing one large chip, chiplet architecture divides computing functions into smaller components that can be integrated within a single package. This enables manufacturers to combine different technologies and potentially reduce design and production costs.
The technology is particularly relevant to the rapid growth of AI and data-centre computing. The Semiconductor Industry Association estimates that the HBM market alone could reach $21 billion in 2025, reflecting the growing need for advanced memory and packaging solutions in AI systems.
The investment is also notable because Italy identified €4 billion in resources for its national microelectronics strategy, covering investment attraction, research and industrial development. Consequently, Novara could support Europe in developing capabilities beyond traditional wafer fabrication, particularly for AI, high-performance computing and next-generation automotive electronics.
Market Stats
- The Italian semiconductor market was valued at US$5.02 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach approximately US$8.76 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 5.70%.
- AI market: Italy’s AI market reached €1.8 billion (~$2.0B) in 2025, growing 50% year-on-year.
- AI adoption: 71% of large Italian companies had launched at least one AI project in 2025.
- AI ecosystem: Italy has 1,010 companies offering AI solutions and 135 AI startups funded over the past five years.
- Semiconductor market: Italy’s semiconductor sector is expected to generate approximately $2.3 billion in revenue in 2025, with STMicroelectronics as the dominant national player. Electronic components: Italy’s electronic-components market reached approximately $12.8 billion in 2025, with imports accounting for 68.4% of market size.
- Data centres: Italy had 513 MW of installed data-centre IT capacity in 2024, up 17% year-on-year. More than €10 billion (US$11.2 billion) of investment was expected for 2025-26.
Strengthening Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain
Silicon Box’s planned facility in Novara can be viewed as part of Europe’s broader effort to reduce vulnerabilities in a semiconductor industry still heavily concentrated outside the region. The European Commission estimates that East Asia accounts for 56% of global front-end wafer-fabrication capacity, while Europe represents only 9%. More broadly, Europe has around 10% of the global semiconductor market, despite having strong capabilities in research, equipment, automotive and industrial chips.

This imbalance matters because semiconductor disruptions can affect entire manufacturing industries. The European Commission notes that some European countries experienced car-production declines of up to one-third during the 2020-22 chip shortage. At the same time, automotive and industrial applications are particularly important to Europe: automotive chips account for 37% of European semiconductor demand, while industrial applications represent another 28%.
Its importance therefore extends beyond Italy. By adding capacity in a previously limited segment of Europe’s semiconductor value chain, the project could diversify sourcing, strengthen links between chip designers and manufacturers, and support European demand for AI, high-performance computing and electric-vehicle technologies. This complements the EU Chips Act’s target of increasing Europe’s global semiconductor share from 10% to 20% by 2030.
Why Italy is backing the investment
The primary purpose of the investment is to strengthen Italy’s domestic semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech manufacturing, reduce vulnerabilities in critical supply chains and support Europe’s technological independence.
Italy is also seeking to position itself as a production platform for the wider digital economy. Italian Industry Minister Adolfo Urso described the project as reinforcing the country's role as a productive platform for the digital economy.
The government has also designated Silicon Box's investment as a project of strategic national interest. Italy has developed mechanisms to accelerate major strategic investments, particularly those involving foreign companies and technologies considered important to national industrial competitiveness.
For Silicon Box, establishing a European manufacturing base provides access to one of the world's largest industrial markets while allowing the company to develop advanced packaging capabilities closer to European customers.
Italy’s Government AI Policy
Italy has developed a national AI policy focused on innovation, competitiveness and responsible use. Its Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 concentrates on four areas: research, public administration, businesses and education/training. The strategy aims to strengthen domestic AI research, encourage companies to adopt AI and improve government services through digital technologies.
In September 2025, Italy approved its national AI law, establishing a framework aligned with the EU AI Act. The legislation emphasises human oversight, transparency, cybersecurity, privacy and accountability, with rules covering healthcare, employment, education, justice and public administration. AgID and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) were designated as key national AI authorities.
A major economic component is a €1 billion (US$1.12 billion) investment programme supporting AI, cybersecurity and related emerging technologies, particularly startups and SMEs. Digital Transformation Department
Overall, Italy’s approach combines regulation with industrial policy, seeking to develop domestic AI capabilities while ensuring that adoption remains secure, transparent and human-centred. This policy direction also complements Italy’s wider investment in semiconductors, digital infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Opportunities for equipment and technology suppliers
- Strong packaging demand: Global assembly and packaging equipment sales grew 21% in 2025, while test-equipment billings increased by 55%, driven partly by AI-related demand.

BRUSSELS — A defeat for Pedro Sánchez in Spain’s snap election risks destabilizing the EU by putting the Socialists and Democrats on the back foot in Brussels and pushing them into a more confrontational stance.
Sánchez, the only Socialist-aligned leader currently running a large EU country, has provided a center-left counterweight to decisions in a Council largely dominated by the center right. Spain’s lawmakers form the S&D’s largest national delegation in the European Parliament, and when Sánchez strikes a Council deal, Spanish MEPs can usually carry his position through the group, even over internal opposition.
A change of government in Madrid would disrupt that arrangement, senior S&D lawmakers told POLITICO. Polls suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, which would likely partner with the far-right Vox party.

articles.title: Discovery of light-activated proteins and their application in neuroscience wins Nobel prize in medicine - Chemistry World
articles.summary: Discovery of light-activated proteins and their application in neuroscience wins Nobel prize in medicine  Chemistry WorldNobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain  BBCHow pond algae led to a Nobel prize and a new way to study the brain  The ConversationNobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 - Prize announcement  NobelPrize.orgUS and German scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on light and brain  Reuters
articles.full_text:
The 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine has been awarded to three researchers for discoveries relating to a class of light-sensitive proteins and how they can control the activity of individual cells. In particular, expressing these proteins in nerve cells has enabled neuroscientists to study which circuits in the brain are responsible for different behaviours, and to develop treatments for various neurological conditions.
The Nobel committee awarded the prize to Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University, US, Peter Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany, and Georg Nagel at the University of Würzburg, Germany, for ‘their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’.
In the early 1990s at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsried, Germany, Hegemann was studying the algae Chlamydomonas, which swims towards light. By attaching small electrodes to the cell’s surface, he was able to measure the electrical signals in the algae’s eyespot – an organelle that contains the light capturing-molecule retinal. However, to study this process in more detail, Hegmann attempted to isolate the light-active proteins with which the retinal interacts. While initially unsuccessful, he eventually identified two genes associated with the proteins.
Meanwhile, at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, Nagel was investigating similar proteins. In 1995, Nagel had used egg cells from the African clawed frog to produce and study bacteriorhodopsin – a light-driven proton pump.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel combined their expertise, inserting the two genes from Chlamydomona into frog eggs. This method produced the light-activated proteins – known as channelrhodopsins – on the cell’s surface. Shining light on these proteins caused a channel to open, letting ions flow into the cell and creating an electrical signal. The pair repeated their experiments with human and hamster kidney cells, finding that they also produced an electrical impulse when exposed to light.
A few years later, Nagel and Deisseroth introduced the same genes into rat nerve cells cultured in a petri dish. Under blue light, the cells produced a signal that spread to other nerve cells. In 2007, Deisseroth’s group took the concept further by activating nerve cells in the brains of live mice. This laid the foundation for the field of optogenetics, in which light is used to activate and study neural circuits.
Following the prize announcement, Abdel El Manira, a neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute, Sweden and a member of the Nobel committee, said that optogenetics has ‘transformed neuroscience’. He notes that researchers are now able to study the link between nerve signals and complex behaviours, such as anxiety, fear and thirst.
‘The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain,’ he added. Researchers are actively looking to use optogenetics to develop treatments for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.

articles.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU - TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU  TechCrunch
articles.full_text:
OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post.
The EU AI Act’s transparency rules, which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify.
OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch.
The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on.
OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key.
Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect.
“These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company.
OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI.
“[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said.
The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users, who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.”
OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.
Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content.

The dollar index (DXY00) rallied to a 1.5-year high on Monday and finished up by +0.23%. The dollar moved higher on Monday amid increased safe-haven demand as political turmoil in France and Spain weighed on the euro. Higher T-note yields on Monday also strengthened the dollar’s interest rate differentials after the 10-year T-note yield rose to a 24-year high of 5.35%. The dollar added to its gains on Monday after the prices paid sub-index of the Sep ISM services index rose more than expected to a 4-year high, a hawkish factor for Fed policy.
Dollar gains were limited on Monday after WTI crude oil fell more than 1%, easing inflation expectations that could persuade the Fed to ease monetary policy, a negative factor for the dollar.

articles.title: Our approach to EU text provenance rules - OpenAI
articles.summary: Our approach to EU text provenance rules  OpenAI
articles.full_text:
Content provenance helps people understand where content came from, how it was created or edited, and whether it contains signals associated with our models. We’ve already made tools publicly available to identify images and audio generated by our models. Today, we’re sharing our approach to text watermarking in response to the EU AI Act, and how it fits into our broader work.
The EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to make generated text identifiable in a machine-readable way. Text watermarking and detection remain early technologies with significant limitations, and views about their benefits and responsible uses are still developing. Our phased approach reflects both the EU AI Act requirements as well as the technology’s limitations, with an emphasis on transparency about what a text watermark can and cannot tell people:
- Starting today, API customers globally will be able to opt in to text watermarking for select models. Text watermarking will remain off by default in the API.
- Over the coming weeks, we will add an invisible watermark to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union.
- We’re opening applications to access our text watermark detector. Access will initially be limited to approved researchers and expert organizations that can help us evaluate and improve the technology. 
  - The above only applies to text provenance—our verification tools for audio and images, including our openai.com/verify web tool and our Content Provenance API(opens in a new window), will continue to be publicly accessible to organizations looking to understand whether an image or audio file was generated by one of our systems.
Our text watermarking technology, textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark. More details about how textGrain works can be found in our technical report(opens in a new window), which will be updated with additional details in the coming weeks. We also plan to make the technology available in open source so that others can build on it.
In our evaluations, textGrain matched or exceeded the performance of other approaches we tested, including SynthID for text. Even so, strong performance under ideal conditions does not guarantee reliable detection in everyday use.
Detectors can make two kinds of errors: they can report a watermark where none is present—a false positive—or miss a watermark that is present—a false negative. Our evaluations below illustrate some of the challenges:
- Shorter or more constrained text is harder to detect. At a target false positive rate of 1%, our detector identified watermarks in about 80% of 200-token passages, compared with about 95% of 400-token passages, for content such as psychology. Detection rates were substantially lower for content such as mathematics, where there is less flexibility in word choice.
- Editing can weaken the watermark. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing 10% of words with synonyms reduced detection from about 92% to 66%. Replacing 25% of words reduced it to 17%.
These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses.
Across the benchmarks we use to assess Astra, our latest frontier model, we do not see meaningful performance differences with and without watermarking.
Text watermarks provide a limited signal about the role our systems played in a passage. It’s important to understand what can and cannot be concluded from a detection result.
- A watermark does not measure human contribution. It can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it.
- A watermark does not establish ownership or responsibility. It does not determine who owns the text, whether its use was lawful, whether disclosure was required, or who is responsible for it.
- A watermark does not identify the user. It does not associate a person, organization, account, prompt, or conversation with the text.
- A watermark does not verify accuracy. It does not tell you whether a passage is true, misleading, harmful, or presented in the right context.
- The absence of a detected watermark does not prove human authorship. Text generated with OpenAI tools may be too short, edited, or translated for detection to work reliably. It may also come from an unsupported model, predate watermarking, or have been generated by another company’s tools.
- Rolling out text watermarking in the EU. Over the coming weeks, we will introduce text watermarking to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users across all plans in the EU only. We are not making text watermarking a global default at launch. This regional approach gives us room to learn from real-world use and feedback.
- Enabling opt-in watermarking for API customers. Starting today, API customers around the world will be able to opt in to watermarked text outputs for select models. This lets customers decide how watermarking fits their transparency obligations and the experiences they provide to users. We are also working with cloud partners to make watermarking available for OpenAI model outputs accessed through their services in the coming weeks.
- Providing detector access to researchers and expert organizations. Approved researchers and expert organizations can apply starting today. In accordance with the Code of Practice(opens in a new window), access will be initially granted on a case-by-case basis to support evaluation and improvement of text provenance. The tool will report whether it detects an OpenAI watermark, without identifying the user or revealing their prompts or conversations. Given the risk of missed watermarks and false positives, we are not making it publicly available at launch.
We expect to revisit each part of this approach as the technology, standards, and evidence evolve.
No single provenance technique is enough on its own, so we take a layered approach that combines open standards, durable watermarking, and verification tools.
We add Content Credentials to supported image outputs, are C2PA conformant(opens in a new window), embed invisible SynthID(opens in a new window) watermarks in supported images and audio, and make image and audio verification available through openai.com/verify and our Content Provenance API(opens in a new window). These techniques complement one another: Content Credentials can record a file’s origin and history, while invisible watermarks can preserve a signal when metadata is removed.
As we described in our election safeguards work, provenance can help people and platforms assess potentially misleading AI-generated content, including deepfakes. We pair these signals with policies, abuse detection, reporting, investigations, and enforcement, and work with researchers, standards bodies, platforms, and civil society to make provenance useful across the wider ecosystem.
Extending provenance to text requires accounting for how easily it can be rewritten, translated, or edited. As we discussed in June, our approach must reflect the practical limits of current technology. We’ll continue improving detection, studying how watermarks withstand editing and translation, and exploring ways to distinguish AI assistance from AI authorship more meaningfully. We’ll adapt our approach as evidence, standards, and regulatory requirements evolve, and expand detector access when we believe results can be interpreted responsibly.
For more information, please visit our help center article(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Female AI agents would get paid 10% less than male ones, study finds - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Female AI agents would get paid 10% less than male ones, study finds  Euronews.comDoes the gender pay gap extend to AI? New University of Limerick research finds female AI agents ‘paid’ less  EurekAlert! Science News ReleasesPeople Paid Male AI Agent More For The Same Work, Study Finds  ForbesHackers access data of 8.8 million people in Denmark in 'extremely serious' breach  Inbox.euStudy Finds Gender Pay Gap in Human Interactions with AI Agents &nbsp...
articles.full_text:
Humans tend to trust and would pay male-presenting AI agents more than female ones for the same work, according to a new study by the University of Limerick on how humans interact with agents in the workplace.
A new study on how people interact with AI agents in the workplace has found that those with a female appearance or presenting as female would get paid less than their male-presenting counterparts for the same work, revealing that gender can influence interactions with artificial intelligence.
The findings come just as AI agents are entering the mainstream, with almost 79% of companies reporting the use of AI agents this year and a further 40% of applications using them too, according to IT consulting firm Accelirate.
This means that if you are not already working with an AI agent, you probably will be soon.
The study, conducted by the University of Limerick and called ‘Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR' aimed to see how humans interact with AI agent co-workers.
Researchers placed 189 human workers in a virtual reality office and tasked them with completing workplace tasks with four different AI assistants.
Among their options were a text-based chatbot, a desk robot, and two human-like agents presented with male and female appearances: Johan and Johanna.
All the assistants had the same background functionality and used the same underlying model, OpenAI’s gpt-4-1106-preview.
Human participants were then asked to rate the AI agents’ work and given real money to pay them for completing tasks, with the aim of recreating a real-world scenario to see how much people were willing to pay AI agents for their work.
Overall, participants rated both human-like agents Johan and Johanna similarly for their work, with Johan trusted marginally more but not by any statistically significant margin.
However, both men and women paid the female-presenting AI agent Johanna significantly less than Johan (10%), despite her having the same capabilities. Johan was also seen as more human-like than Johanna.
This is despite most participants telling researchers in interviews that they would not treat male and female-presenting AI agents differently.
Fortunately for Johan and Johanna, they were both paid more for their work than the other AI agents, with women in particular scoring and rewarding the human-presenting agents more than men did.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, participants also saw both human-presenting AI agents as much more human-like than the chatbot and robot.
Not only that, workers trusted and credited Johan and Johanna more than the other AI agents, with women in particular trusting them more than men.
“Having Johanna next to me made me more prone to credit her more again because I felt there was a person, a colleague sitting next to me that I had a conversation with and that was giving me her own input,” said one participant.
The study also found that people preferred AI agents that were either human-presenting or clearly non-human presenting, rejecting the robot design that appeared to be “in between” the two options.
Outside of the gender dynamics, those who took part in the study said that “AI assistants should integrate seamlessly into every knowledge work to be useful”.

articles.full_text:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called a snap election for Nov. 29, a vote that could signal the demise of the EU’s last major Socialist government and remove one of Europe’s chief critics of U.S. President Donald Trump from the political front line.
Already weakened by the corruption cases battering his Socialist Party, Sánchez took a further knock this summer when he faced fierce blowback over his handling of the ongoing migrant crisis in the North African exclave of Ceuta.
But the bitter topic of unaffordable housing — something that tops the list of voters’ concerns in Spain and which has sparked nationwide protests — has finally prompted Sánchez to call an early election in an apparent bid to seize a campaign battleground he believes could work to his advantage.

articles.title: On a remote Greek island, empty classrooms signal a crisis across Europe - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.summary: On a remote Greek island, empty classrooms signal a crisis across Europe  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

source_detail.name: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

articles.full_text:
Greece’s remote islands are becoming a warning sign of Europe’s population decline, as falling birth rates and youth migration threaten schools and local communities
KALAMOS, Greece -- Chryssa Ntalaka's classroom has become an object lesson in subtraction.
The sole teacher in the last school on the idyllic Greek island of Kalamos has a shorter list of students every fall. This year, just two. On Sept. 23, the sixth graders sat at Ntalaka’s table beneath the whiteboard, in front of rows of unused desks and benches.
When they head to middle school on Greece’s mainland next year, her school will be mothballed. Toys and picture books still sit on shelves in the nearby kindergarten since it was shuttered three years ago.
“Usually, teachers are placed on these islands against their wishes,” Ntalaka told The Associated Press. “Whereas for Kalamos there are teachers and kindergarten teachers, as far as I know, who want to come — but there are no children.”
Falling enrollment across Greece this year prompted authorities to close 75 schools and suspend or extend suspension of classes at more than 400 others.
It’s a situation playing out across Europe and beyond. The region has 16 of the world's top 20 oldest nations, particularly in Southern Europe, according to the independent World Population Review.
And its remote communities act as an early warning system: Mountain villages and small islands are among the first places where schools and services disappear in a deepening cycle of population decline. Some 17 million people live on more than 4,000 islands across the European Union; Greece has about 200 of them.
“Closing schools leads to young people not staying and to them leaving,” said Byron Kotzamanis, co-founder of the Institute of Demographic Research in Athens. “Leaving means fewer and fewer people — fewer and fewer births. It means depopulation and dead settlements that will become nursing homes.”
Kalamos' year-round population is just 80. A decade ago, it had 40 children in local schools and public daycare.
“It was very nice. We played together every day. We went to (primary) school every morning,” Antonis Aivaliotis, a high school senior, said during a ferry ride in the predawn light.
Aivaliotis is among Kalamos’ seven teenagers who today make a choppy crossing to school on the mainland. They miss class on days when strong winds pose a risk.
He spent several years as a student of Ntalaka’s class, which at the time was a single room with children of all ages.
Ntalaka has often been the lone teacher during her 20 years at remote schools. Half that time was in Kalamos, located not far from Odysseus’ home island Ithaca in “The Odyssey.”
She fell in love with Kalamos' unspoiled beaches that are a magnet for yacht tourists. She learned to dive and became an accomplished spearfisher. But she will have to leave.
All it would take for her school to remain open would be the arrival of two families. She and town officials have desperately sought to spread the word, but there’s no sign of any comers.
“We’re very welcoming and we’re trying. That’s what we want to do, even right now — for someone to hear us,” Ntalaka said. “The sooner, the better.”
As for Aivaliotis, he sees moving away after graduation as an inevitability.
“Of course I would like to stay here,” he said. “I love Kalamos. It is my home. But there’s no development at all.”
Aging countries are struggling to keep their island schools open, with limited success.
Croatia has invested 4.6 billion euros ($5.1 billion) in its islands over the past 10 years, Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said in June. That includes 20 kindergartens being built or expanded, and renovation of primary schools and sports arenas. Croatia's parliament, the Sabor, in January passed an Islands Act aimed at improving life for islanders. The rate of population decline on small, remote Croatian islands is similar to that of the mainland.
Japan faces grimmer demographics. In the decade through 2023, the population of over 250 remote islands covered by a government support program fell 19%, almost double the national rate, according to the most-recent government data. Nearly 1 million people lived on those islands in 1955, and 340,000 by 2020.
This has led to a shortage of people to operate ferries and other transportation, worsening economic contraction on remote islands. Japan’s government says maintaining residents is crucial to national security and has provided subsidies to lure people to work in tourism, fishing and other industries.
Some islands have managed to recruit students from elsewhere. On remote Oki Islands, for example, 74 of the 132 students at a fisheries high school were drawn there through family relocation programs.
And on the Italian island of Stromboli, formed by the tip of a volcano, a school reopened last month after 20 years with a single student. Italian elementary schools normally need at least 15 pupils, but exceptions are granted to remote islands because a school's closure can accelerate depopulation.
Images broadcast on Italian television showed 6-year-old Aysha wearing a purple backpack almost as big as her body and holding her mom’s hand as she walked through the narrow streets of Ginostra to her first class inside the village's local church.
Aris Alexopoulos, head of the OECD’s Crete Center on Population Dynamics, says Greece’s population will fall as low as 8 million, from 10.5 million, by 2050. Young people are becoming a minority, he said on the sidelines of a demographics conference in Athens on Sept. 21.
The trend extends across the European Union: 3.55 million babies were born in 2024, roughly half the 1964 peak. Its fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.34 children per woman, well below the 2.1 level needed to maintain a stable population. Greece was among few countries with rates below 1.25.
In June, the EU announced it would develop a strategy for islands, aiming to address the problem of shrinking populations, among others.
Themis Christophidou, director-general for regional and urban policy at the European Commission, told AP in an email that the EU has spent 146 million euros ($164 million) over the past five years to modernize schools on four Greek island clusters, specifically to counter demographic decline.
“Mobility is one of Europe’s strengths, but people should leave by choice, never because of neglect or missing investment,” she wrote. “That starts with quality public services, with education at their heart.”
___
Gatopoulos reported from Athens, Greece. Associated Press journalists Theodora Tongas in Athens, Greece, Menelaos Hadjicostis in Nicosia, Cyprus, Giada Zampano in Rome and Mari Yamaguchi and Yuri Kageyama in Tokyo contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego - BBC
articles.summary: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego  BBCLA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them  The GuardianTrump: Let Iran take out LA with a nuclear bomb  The TelegraphTrump’s comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego was incoherent, not malicious  CNNNow Trump has abandoned his fellow Americans – will America abandon him?  The i Paper
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.
The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

articles.title: Hull EV driver says street charging is a 'postcode lottery' - BBC
articles.summary: Hull EV driver says street charging is a 'postcode lottery'  BBCAndy Burnham brings in 'pavement tax' for one group of Brits – costing £200  Daily StarAndy Burnham's driveway decision that's costing some UK EV drivers £389  AOL.comGovernment lays regulations to relax permitted development rules for electric vehicle infrastructure  Planning ResourcePublic charging cost threatens EV adoption, say half of dealers  Motor Trade News
articles.full_text:
Terraced street EV charging 'postcode lottery'
Sean says he breaks the law every time he charges his electric car outside his terraced home in Hull because access to charging is a "postcode lottery".
The 51-year-old bought his EV through the Motability scheme two years ago despite knowing he could not charge on his street, but hoped new infrastructure would make it easier for people without driveways to charge at home.
Unable to install a wall-mounted charger because it would require council permission, he instead uses a cable running across the pavement overnight.
A Hull City Council spokesperson said: "Under existing legislation, it is illegal to place a rope, wire or similar apparatus across a highway without consent."
The local authority is developing a policy on cross-pavement charging, but Sean says changes have not come quickly enough.
"I knew that it was going to be a problem, but it's one that hopefully the government was going to try and solve for people," he said.
"I just didn't expect it to take as long as it is and it's very different depending on where you live so it's a bit of a postcode lottery, but I knew it was the right decision for us because of the cost-effectiveness of it, especially as you can see the prices of fuel going up as they are at the moment."
Sean, a carer who looks after two adults, mainly charges his car at a nearby hospital and public charging sites during the day, but uses a "granny charger" from a domestic mains supply to top up his car overnight.
Charging at home is generally cheaper than using public charging points. Households on a standard variable electricity tariff currently pay an average of 26.32p per kilowatt-hour for electricity, while Hull City Council's public charging network charges 30p per kilowatt-hour and chargers at Hull Royal Infirmary are listed at 33p per kilowatt-hour, with parking charges paid separately.
Sean said he minimises the time the covered cables are across the path, putting them out late at night and removing them early in the morning.
"You have to be a bit clever with how you do it, obviously you can't have trailing wires and trip hazards so I have covers that go over it and I've written to the council several times to ask to be part of the pilot scheme."
When challenged about breaking the law, Sean said: "It doesn't feel comfortable, because at any moment you can get a letter through the post saying that you're doing something, and I'm taking a risk talking about that I do it now.
"But something has to change, and the only way that the council's going to do that is if people raise it up."
Under the Highways Act 1980, people are prohibited from placing a cable over the "highway" and are liable to a fine if found guilty. In addition, people who cause injury by trailing a cable could face civil action.
The Wheelchair Alliance said charging cables crossing pavements could create additional obstacles for wheelchair users.
Nick Goldup, chief executive of The Wheelchair Alliance, said: "Wheelchair users already face numerous accessibility challenges when navigating our streets and pavements, from poorly maintained surfaces to the growing number of e-scooters and hire bikes.
"We have previously called upon the Department for Transport to consider the impact these increasing obstacles can have on wheelchair users and charging cables potentially add another barrier."
A Hull City Council spokesperson said: "Whilst the Council is investigating future measures that could provide residents with convenient charging options, it is not currently the case that residents in the city are authorised to trail an electric vehicle cable across a public pavement.
"As the highway authority, Hull City Council does not permit this because it could cause a potential trip hazard."
Hull City Council has been awarded more than £2.8m from the government's Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (LEVI) fund to help deliver more on-street residential charging and fast-charging points across the area.
The council said the final review of contracts was taking place before final submission for approval, but it could not give a timeframe for when installation work would begin.
In neighbouring East Riding of Yorkshire, residents can register interest in having a gully installed in the footpath outside their homes to allow charging cables to run below the surface.
East Riding of Yorkshire Council said 52 people had applied so far, although no formal decision had been made on whether to progress with a scheme.
According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), 26.2% of all vehicles sold in the first half of 2026 were electric.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said the growing choice of models being made available combined with high fuel prices meant more people were likely to be considering a switch.
Simon Williams, head of policy for the RAC, said: "The government has actually made it a lot easier now to actually install EV chargers in terraced homes, and you can potentially run a cable under the pavement with permission without having to get permission from the council these days.
"So things are getting better from that point of view. But there's obviously no guarantee you can actually park outside your home."
